Two primary methods for detecting financial bubbles based on rational expectations and positive feedback traps are investigated, including the use of temporal bubble indicators and a diagnostic test for bubble initiation. Our theoretical framework involves two parties, one creating assets and the other acquiring them, with each acting rationally and anticipating the actions of the other. Expectations are adaptive and influenced by past performance. Temporal bubble indicators express the excess returns over an assumed minimum return threshold, while the diagnostic test identifies the point at which a bubble transitions from unlikely to probable. Our results indicate that indicators derived from cumulative returns and a diagnostic test that is both optimistic and conservative in nature can identify bubbles with near perfect accuracy. However, this performance degrades as model parameters shift towards more volatile market conditions characterized by higher expectations for returns and longer anticipated waiting times for assets. Due to the stochastic nature of task completion times, which are inherently discrete and discrete-time independent, traditional statistical tests are inapplicable. Consequently, traditional statistical tests are replaced by a hybrid approach that combines empirical results and theoretical probabilities, resulting in a modified test that is conservative, optimistic, and reliable in its assessment, exhibiting greater efficiency in its application compared to standard procedures.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either no driving force or an external driving force using path integral techniques. A novel set of algorithms based on Markov chain Monte Carlo methods was developed for path integral calculations of systems under external driving forces. Unlike existing methods, this approach involves simulating only the effects of a single driving force term at a specific moment in time. Consequently, this method exhibits a level of detail that resembles second-order perturbation theory, yet it avoids explicitly propagating oscillators' wave functions. Furthermore, we discovered that, when there is no driving force, our method aligns with other path integral methods. When the driving force level increased, our calculations of key quantities such as the average energy, a thermal expectation value of the position squared, and a thermal expectation value of the momentum squared showed a notable alignment with the expected behavior from perturbation theory. All these results were achieved with relatively simple underlying distributions of oscillator states.

Recent research has shown significant progress in improving recommender system performance through leveraging reviews for predicting ratings, however the current methods have several limitations. The existing techniques often use complex neural networks, which make it challenging to easily understand reviewer sentiments. Moreover, they tend to overlook the unique interaction between reviews and users/items, where each review contributes differently to modeling user/item preferences. To overcome these challenges, a new approach called Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) has been proposed for review-based item recommendations. The method starts by encoding user/item reviews using BERT and introduces a sentiment extraction module to capture review sentiment scores and distribution patterns. A novel review-aware interactive module then synergizes review features, user/item embeddings, and sentiment scores to generate informative review representations. Finally, a review-based matching module aggregates these informative review representations to produce a strong signal for predicting ratings. The approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several real-world datasets, showcasing its effectiveness.

Developing NLP systems for Code-Switched Text is an extremely challenging task due to the complex nature of multiple languages involved in it. Data augmentation has been proven to be an effective method in overcoming this difficulty, requiring thorough comprehension of the target code-mixing characteristics. In our research, we investigated the effects of lexical replacement on data augmentation in CS text. We presented novel techniques to create CS dataset variants by replacing CS words with those from other languages. We used two distance metrics - Levenshtein and BLEU - to measure the text modification impact. Our experiments involved replacing CS words in Arabic-English data with both original and translated words, showing that utilizing both native and translated replacement lexical sets enhances the diversity of CS data. We found that our data augmentation approach raised the word error rate by 15.63% and 16.23% for the two sets, respectively, without decreasing the language modeling accuracy.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

We're investigating integrable boundary conditions that can be geometrically interpreted as D-branes within specific theoretical models based on products of group- and coset-spaces, which are generalized versions of lambda deformations. Utilizing a sigma-model approach, we found that all the established conformal brane systems in the context of products of WZW models are preserved under the lambda deformations, with some transitioning into new, equivalent boundary states. We also discovered that the boundary states corresponding to the A-type WZW models, which could not be explicitly solved for the generalized products, are preserved as well. A cross-check of our findings used a holographic duality concept called bulk-boundary correspondence.

The selection of a mesh topology directly influences its suitability for specific simulation methods such as the Finite Element Method. A novel algorithm introduces variations on the Tetrahedralization of Hex meshes, which typically consist of hexahedra and higher-order cells. Such meshes often contain irregular, non-regular topologies with repeating patterns not present in standard type II meshes. To address this, the algorithm converts these non-regular topologies into viable configurations for various hex-based simulations. It has a time complexity of O(n log n) and processes each element in the mesh independently, allowing for efficient implementation. In cases of optimal conditions, the algorithm's time efficiency can be reduced to nearly linear, specifically to O(n log
log n), through the use of memory caching. This optimization was confirmed in the mesh untangling process that precedes FEM simulations, which demonstrated an average time efficiency of 44.17 Tets/Hex with a peak of 58 at optimal conditions. Additionally, the algorithm was tested on a dataset of 2198 models from the MeshGallery library, as well as four other datasets consisting of meshes with irregular cell topologies.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task
approach, training existing relation extraction models alongside knowledge graph
link prediction to ultimately boost the models' overall performance and achieve
predictable gains in accuracy.

This study introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically designed for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Developed with flexibility in mind, this delay model can be tailored to accommodate a wide range of process technologies. One of the key challenges in constructing a reliable delay model lies in accurately characterizing the non-linear inverter behavior. To overcome this complexity, the proposed model employs a parameterization technique that is both comprehensive and straightforward. By relying on just three key parameters, this model offers a significant reduction in the complexity of the parameterization. These parameters can be easily determined using a variety of analytical methods, including corner simulations. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through its compatibility with the IEEE 12304 standard. Furthermore, the study showcases the utility of Matlab's Curve Fitting Toolbox in facilitating parameterization.

Making optimal decisions in complex, continuously changing environments with
insufficient information is a challenging task in many scenarios. To overcome
this issue, we suggest a novel theoretical approach rooted in the Rademacher
chaos theory. This framework enables us to identify the inherent complexity of
metric-space-based reinforcement learning problems. Building upon our findings,
we identify the most basic level of simplicity and develop simple, efficient
algorithms that leverage this complexity reduction. Additionally, we extend
existing reliability bounds for these simplified models, demonstrating their
utility in the real-world by comparing their performance to state-of-the-art
reward-learning algorithms in metric spaces.

The underlying mechanisms of the primate ventral temporal cortex's animacy detection network are not fully understood, despite their crucial role in guiding attention and behavior. Research utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging has revealed a distinct animacy-related activation pattern in the anterior parts of the left temporal fusiform junction when comparing animate to inanimate objects, and further findings show that this pattern is present not only in humans but also in macaques. However, the exact structural composition of this animacy network remains a topic of debate. We propose that it consists of multiple distinct components, including a common left temporal fusiform junction foundation found in both humans and macaques, as well as separate regions for face and body recognition, animal species-specificity, and a broader area encompassing both temporal and parietal regions.

In scientific simulation, achieving accurate replication of real-world scenarios is a top priority. However, commonly used methods such as the finite element method and finite volume method are often prone to inaccuracies and artifacts, like Gibbs oscillations, particularly when simulating complex, multi-dimensional systems. This issue can be addressed by employing advanced filtering techniques, like the C^0 quadrature filter, which help maintain the overall structure of the solution. These filtering methods work by reducing the high-frequency components of the solution, using its surrounding values to fill in the missing data. This can be achieved by solving an optimization problem that conforms to specific mesh constraints, making the solution smooth and consistent within the grid structures. This paper introduces a new filtering approach, the structure-preserving quadrature filter, which conforms to specific mesh constraints in a way that's similar to the C^0 quadrature filter. This filter is characterized by the use of weighted, high-frequency values from specific grid points to maintain the solution's overall structure and ensure its accuracy. The SPAQF is defined as a quadratic programming problem with linear constraints that are tied to the mesh structure. The results show that the SPAQF is able to accurately replicate real-world scenarios in both 1D and 2D systems, while also outperforming existing filters by reducing errors and artifacts at similar computational costs.

Quasi-periodic oscillations type C, typically observed in low-hard and hard-intermediate states of black hole X-ray transients, have been investigated using the MAXI J1535-571 data collected by Insight-HXMT. By applying a novel time-dependent Comptonization model and a relativistic reflection model, researchers have demonstrated its ability to accurately describe X-ray data up to 100 keV. The model shows that the corona's electron density significantly changes, decreasing by two orders, as the source transitions from the hard-intermediate to soft-intermediate state. Furthermore, researchers have observed a correlation between the corona's size and the 13 second QPO period, suggesting that the corona is likely to be limited by these QPOs, implying a transition boundary which may facilitate mass transfer between the corona and the disk.

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to deviation from optimal strategies. This often manifests as suboptimal action choices in partner-dependent tasks, causing agents to adopt a'self-centered' approach. To address this challenge, a novel method employing intrinsic motivation based on transfer empowerment is proposed, which maximizes the capabilities of the agent in various partner configurations. Through the introduction of a maximum eigenvalue of the joint covariance matrix as a reward signal, the agent's focus shifts to actions that enhance its partner-dependent joint action capabilities. Theoretical underpinnings demonstrate that partner empowerment-based rewards facilitate a convergence of optimal joint actions in a range of symmetric cooperative tasks. Experimental validation, utilizing a set of asymmetric cooperative tasks characterized by dynamic partner behaviors, reveals that the proposed transfer empowerment reward results in a robust and generalizable joint action policy, distinguishing it from the random exploration and reward maximization approaches demonstrated in the experiments.

We introduce MatSim, a comprehensive synthetic dataset, benchmark, and 
approach designed to leverage computer vision for identifying and 
transferring similarities and transitions across materials and textures. 
MatSim enables one-shot learning, empowering the identification of any 
material regardless of the context or circumstances using only one or 
multiple examples. The material categories in MatSim are extensive, numerous 
(101), and finely granular, allowing for seamless application to a wide 
range of scenarios. 
A key innovation in MatSim is its adoption of a self-supervised 
contrastive learning framework, effectively harnessing a dataset with 
labelled categories without resorting to labels for individual examples. 
Additionally, MatSim employs a unique rendering technique that generates 
realistic images by incorporating the material's geographical context, 
enabling the introduction of nuanced environmental influences during 
training. The MatSim benchmark showcases the approach's robustness by 
demonstrating generalization across multiple datasets and scenarios, 
including one-shot learning from limited data, similarity classification, 
and extrapolation to unfamiliar environments.

Two equivalent formulations of Lie 2-algebras are examined: one as a categorification of Lie algebras and another as 2-term L∞-algebras. The discussion includes examples, cohomology, and the Serre-Swartz theorem. The paper delves into four equivalent definitions of n-Lie algebras and the skeletal Lie n-algebra concept. It also explores 1-Lie algebras and their connection to Lie groupoids through the adjoint cohomology. The discussion is further expanded to n-multilinear maps and n-Lie groupoids, focusing on the specific cases of 2-Lie groups and crossed modules. The relevant properties and examples of crossed squares of groups are also presented.

We introduce a novel method for local image feature matching, where instead of a time-consuming pixel-by-pixel assessment, we scan images at a more focused level with a detailed examination of key points within smaller regions. By leveraging the advanced computing capabilities of GPUs, we can now efficiently implement this approach at an optimal speed. Our approach, called LoFTR, uses self-attention mechanisms to accurately identify corresponding features in images, while also allowing for flexible scaling of the complex computations involved in such assessments. We test the effectiveness of our approach by comparing it with traditional methods using a range of image datasets, including still images and video footage, demonstrating significantly improved performance and efficiency. Notably, our approach can operate at a remarkable speed of over 100 frames per second on standard hardware.

The SMF measurement is a critical component in solar research, but its accuracy is hampered by observation limitations. Sunspot fields are typically estimated through the force-free idealization, but the method's reliability diminishes with increasing field strength. The implicit assumption behind these estimates carries a risk of significant biases, particularly in the lower-field regime. This study assesses potential biases in BBFF models, considering their impact on magnetic energy storage. The investigation reveals a substantial bias in BBFF models when using open-boundary conditions, but it can be mitigated using a simple adjustment. The magnitude of the bias remains significant even in the range of strong fields typically associated with sunspots, suggesting it could be responsible for the observed correlation between energy storage and field strength. The research also provides insights into the role of modeling constraints in BBFF models, highlighting their importance in determining model quality and potential biases.

This research explores a real-world scenario in which consumers selfishly aim to minimize their energy bills by scheduling their energy usage in advance. To effectively persuade these consumers to use less energy during peak hours and fairly compensate them, we developed a novel billing scheme that instantiates real-time energy usage charges. Initially, we define an aggregative game to simulate how these consumers interact to achieve a mutually beneficial outcome. By employing variational inequality theory, we identify the conditions necessary for the existence and uniqueness of a Nash equilibrium under our proposed instant load pricing (LLP) mechanism. To address the computational complexity of finding the equilibrium, we present a convergent iterative solution method. Moreover, we show that our LLP scheme mirrors the final billing outcome of an optimal, decentralized, variable price mechanism designed to incentivize users to execute their load profiles in advance. To evaluate the performance of our LLP scheme, we conducted numerical case studies on a European household load model.

A semi-classical model for Hawking radiation is developed in the context of Rastall theory of gravity. This theory considers a modification to the divergence free condition in the Einstein tensor. The researchers explore black string and black hole radiation within this framework. They establish that the gravitational field impacts the radiation's particle and antiparticle distributions. Furthermore, analyses on the radiation's number density, trapping potential, and temperature indicate that the Rastall theory of gravity causes Hawking radiation to diminish for both black strings and black holes, with the latter exhibiting more pronounced reductions.

The results demonstrate that the power-law decay rates found in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for discrete systems directly correspond to pointwise scaling rates of a spectral measure with a spectral value of one. Moreover, assuming weak convergence, when no spectral gap is present, the convergence rates of the time-average in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem rely on sequences of infinite time as they tend to infinity.

The Research on Specimen Physics target, a unique star system with extremely rare properties, presents a unique opportunity for astronomical research. However, selecting and analyzing metal-poor stars, key components of the ROSPEC mission, relies on precise iron abundance measurements. These measurements require high-quality spectra, often obtained at a low signal-to-noise ratio. To help achieve the mission's goals, this study develops a method for identifying metal-poor stars using spectra obtained by the BP/RP instrument at Gaia. By combining the IRFU code with synthetic spectra and a temperature-dependent polynomial model, researchers can determine stellar iron abundance. Moreover, the approach can be adapted to various spectral types and ranges. By applying the method to a set of synthetic spectra with differing signal-to-noise ratios, the temperature and iron abundance uncertainties were calculated. Notably, the method's errors remain acceptable below a signal-to-noise ratio of 10. To validate the approach, the researchers compared its results with measurements from three standard stars. The selected target stars for this study were metal-poor stars with known iron abundance values. The method estimated the iron abundance for each target star within an error margin of approximately 0.3-0.5 dex. The research also analyzed a set of known metal-poor stars with iron abundance measured using other methods. The results compared the iron abundance values obtained through the selected method and those measured using other methods. The researchers found a good agreement between the iron abundance values, with a correlation

This research demonstrates the effectiveness of an algorithm designed to evaluate and predict fire season severity worldwide. The number of wildfires and fire-related deaths across the globe has been increasing dramatically during fire seasons, causing significant destruction to property and human life. Accurate estimation of fire severity is essential to efficiently allocate resources for fire management, a task that has traditionally been hampered by data constraints. Our team has developed a data-driven approach to forecast fire severity using historical data, aiming to address this issue. Our algorithm, which utilizes Gaussian Process regression, yields reliable results even with limited data. Case studies from the United States and Australia illustrate the efficacy of our approach. Furthermore, an interactive web platform has been established to provide real-time forecasts of fire severity, enabling informed decision-making through data visualization. The platform's address is https://firespread.org/.

We conducted a study to assess the variability in morphological complexity across 47 languages, using five distinct measures of morphological complexity. These measures were applied to the CLULI corpus, which is based on the morphological analysis of sentences from 47 languages. We compared our findings with existing research on the complexity of languages, collecting data on 47 languages based on characteristics like word order, inflectional complexity, and other factors. Our research demonstrates that several of the corpus-based measures of complexity align with general perceptions of complexity, yet a few fail to offer reliable information. We hypothesize that the discrepancies between the results can be attributed to biases introduced during the data annotation process. The study emphasizes the significance of cross-linguistic data in morphological complexity assessments.

Researchers at Meneghetti et al have discovered an increased occurrence of small gravitational lens effects within galaxy clusters.  To examine its impact, they compared self-interacting dark matter models with standard cold dark matter models.  It was discovered that early-type galaxies in clusters had a higher concentration gradient when compared to late-type clusters, and this pattern persisted across both cold dark dark matter and self-interacting dark matter scenarios.  Additionally, they found that taking into account the movement of objects in clusters did not resolve the discrepancy between observed and simulated gravitational lens effects.  It was also determined that if the mass of objects in clusters was not taken into account correctly, it could result in a large overestimation of the mass of early-type galaxy clusters, and this overestimation became more pronounced in self-interacting dark matter scenarios.  It was concluded that self-interacting dark matter scenarios presented difficulties for standard cold dark matter models could be ruled out through the observation of mass and gravitational lens effects in clusters.

This research focuses on reducing the complexity of parametric partial differential equations (PPDEs) by finding an accurate approximation space for the solutions of the equations. Given incomplete information, we use two primary sources: initial assumptions about the solutions and partial measurements from the equations. Based on these sources, we have developed methods to generate effective approximation subspaces and analyzed their performance. By identifying the optimal performance limit and providing simplified methods to achieve it, we have made strides in addressing the challenges associated with reducing the dimensionality of PPDE solutions while accounting for incomplete information about the equations and their solutions.

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel (m-ar-K) Fast Independent Component Analysis (FastICA) transformation, offering an alternative to the traditional kernel trick that's computationally intensive. By applying the kernel trick to the conventional ICA methodology, it's possible to perform component separation in higher-dimensional spaces. However, this approach incurs additional computational costs. The proposed m-ar-K Fast ICA method mitigates this by leveraging faster ICA algorithms, such as FastICA, and implementing a novel kernel trick technique that replaces the need for explicit mapping to higher-dimensional spaces. Instead, it's based on a kernel-inspired function, derived from the arcsinh term, that's used in conjunction with FastICA. This method also incorporates another innovation: the application of the kernel trick to data samples rather than the traditional approach. Experimental evaluations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed method.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial for numerous applications, such as disaster relief and marketing strategies. The sheer volume of social media data, however, poses significant challenges to processing and analyzing this information quickly. In response, several advanced techniques have been developed to efficiently detect social media events spatially and temporally. Our study focuses on designing an event detection framework that combines data sampling, N-gram modeling, and clustering algorithms to accurately detect social media events within a specified geographic area and time frame in real-time. The framework uses a data sampling approach that incorporates both spatial and temporal conditions to efficiently process social media data. A weighted N-gram algorithm is then applied to identify events across multiple posts. Finally, event clustering is performed using density-based methods to group related events together. The framework's reliability was validated through experiments using real-world social media data. Our study demonstrated that the weighted N-gram model with a time of three years and a distance of 5 km produced the best results, outperforming existing approaches by 15%. The framework's accuracy was further enhanced by temporal filtering and spatial clustering, achieving a 90% accuracy rating.

We establish the optimal Holder continuity for solutions to elliptic equations that integrate volumetric and surface measures, under the condition that the gradient of the source term belongs to the W1,p space. Specifically, for p greater than 1, the associated regularity result states that the solution has enhanced Holder continuity, specifically with a delta-p/2 characteristic, uniformly across the domain. Notably, this result is valid for any p between 1 and infinity and encompasses cases involving measure-generated perturbations. Moreover, assuming an even more stringent condition, namely that the gradient of the source term belongs to the W1,p space for some p greater than 1, a corresponding regularity result can be established, with the Holder continuity characterized by delta min{p/2,1/2} throughout.

Advanced permanent magnets made from rare earth and transition metal alloys achieve high magnetization due to high transition metal content. By utilizing computational searches based on fundamental laws, researchers explored the binary and ternary systems formed by yttrium, cobalt, and boron to discover new materials. This investigation aimed at finding cobalt-rich compounds within the YCo$_{20}$-YCo$_{6}$ phase boundary to create magnetic alloys that could serve as replacements for traditional ferrimagnetic ferrites and replace them in various applications. To conduct the search, known cobalt-rich compounds with a specific crystal structure were utilized as a starting point to develop a chemical potential mu$_{\rm Co}$. By adjusting the chemical potential, the phase space for cobalt-rich compounds with hexagonal close-packed (hcp) and body-centered tetragonal (bct) structures was expanded to allow for variable metal concentrations and different metal sites that could accommodate yttrium and boron. Ultimately, the search identified multiple cobalt-rich intermetallic ferrites with hcp and bct structures and natural boron incorporation into these alloys, resulting in improved magnetic properties compared to traditional ferrites.

In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has become the standard practice. Each ad impression resulting from user interaction is instantly auctioned off, with demand-side platforms (DSPs) providing bids. Typically, DSPs seek to maximize their returns based on the auction strategies they employ, but there are instances where the bids submitted by DSPs fail to match the auction mechanisms used by exchanges. The bids submitted by DSPs are subject to review, with the bid validation rules aimed at preventing fraud and maintaining the quality of the ad distribution process. Nonclassical properties in continuous-variable quantum systems are often marked by quantum correlations and Wigner negativity. This study explores how these two nonclassical traits are connected in the context of a single-mode bosonic field, particularly focusing on steerable states and Wigner negativity in relation to each other. Firstly, we demonstrate that any state displaying quantum steering also exhibits Wigner negativity, and provide examples of nonclassical states devoid of steering. Next, we examine the relationship between steering probability, the amount of Wigner negativity in a state, and the-norm operator. Lastly, we show that locally detecting the steering from an arbitrary state is equivalent to distinguishing certain nonclassical states from the vacuum, with both tasks having equivalent computational complexity.

Accurate secure boundary analysis is crucial for practical quantum key distribution systems, but the current approach overlooks a critical aspect – the randomness consistency of seeds used in privacy amplification. We introduce and prove a quantum leftover hash lemma that applies to non-uniform random seeds, and subsequently establish a detailed secure boundary analysis for quantum key distribution, taking into account varying randomness levels of seeds. Taking the differential phase analysis experiment as an example, we show that by implementing our analytical method, the secure boundary of this experiment can be precisely estimated. Compared to the original analysis, our approach achieves approximately 35% to 41% improvement in key rate, which approaches the theoretical QKD secure boundary, with an average gap of approximately 0.01.

This research involves finding certain types of curves within a higher-dimensional space that have a non-negative metric signature, specifically in the four-dimensional Euclidean space expanded by one extra dimension, and focusing on the properties of d'Alembertian operator for curves that meet specific criteria, including being non-planar and non-spherical.

We'll examine the diffusion process described by the equation $u_t(t, x) =
\tfrac{1}{2}\{x u(t, x)\}_{xx} - \alpha \{x u(t, x)\}_{x}$ with $u(0, x) =
\delta(x - x_0)$ for $t, x, \alpha \ge 0$, initially derived and solved by Feller
for modeling independently reproducing populations where the initial population is
$\alpha$ times that at $t$ zero. This study will derive the probability
distribution associated with taking a sample of size $n$ from such a population
and relate it to the time it takes for two genes from the same population to
coalesce. We'll also provide a detailed analytical study of the diffusion process
and its characteristics.

In monolithic waveguide QED systems without distinct units, we analyze the scattering behavior of multi-photon states, developing an efficient method based on Feynman diagrams. The scattering matrix in these systems, described by a specific type of matrix that rotates states, can be easily calculated from a fundamental set of rules, similar to Fermi theory, by combining any given set of photons. We verify our method by comparing it with exact numerical calculations, demonstrating its effectiveness and showing that it significantly reduces computational complexity, enabling scattering matrix calculations for a wide range of multi-photon states. We further use this framework to investigate the scattering of two photons, observing that it can be linked to the system's eigenstates and used to determine the phase of non-local two-photon correlations, thereby realizing two key elements of quantum computing without needing fine-tuning.

A potential way to study low-mass dark matter is by utilizing boosted dark matter interactions. The framework for light dark matter interactions involving no spin is relatively well-established. However, the same cannot be said for spin-dependent interactions. The current work develops an alternative method for examining these interactions, specifically in proton and neutron targets. By comparing boosted dark matter scattering off free, bound, and nuclear particles with existing direct detection experiments, the impact of dark matter Lorentz factor is evaluated. The new approach considers various dark matter properties and interaction functions. The findings show that by taking into account a wide range of dark matter parameters and interaction functions, the direct detection data from XENON100 can set limits on spin-dependent interactions, particularly at tree-level. The analysis also considers the potential of future XenonPTD and CRESST experiments in boosting our understanding of dark matter interactions in direct detection, as well as the potential of future mobile detector facilities like SPACE and TTVF in exploring new interaction regions. The experiments will be able to cover a wide range of dark matter mass, with its highest sensitivity to low-mass dark matter interactions, particularly below 10 GeV. The new approach using relativistic particles is independent of non-relativistic calculations and can be used in various experiments that involve particle collisions with matter. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances. Nevertheless, its conventional detection method incurs additional delay. This study proposes a novel method to minimize this delay. It commences by redefining the conventional differential detection criterion for a linearly filtered signal. By employing the minimum product of the raised cosine frequency response and time window, the criterion ensures that the signal's spectrum remains within the passband, thereby preventing aliasing in the Fourier transform. Subsequently, the optimal time window is obtained by maximizing the product of a normalized raised cosine frequency response and the time window, for a given delay. This optimization is a convex problem, solvable through the use of the Cholesky decomposition. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing alternatives.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, which presents a complex problem due to the extensive time required for labeling. To address this issue, we have developed a technique that minimizes the necessary number of labels. The foundation of our approach lies in a dense subgraph representation of the reward space, which we then rank using various criteria to determine optimal cluster boundaries. To establish these clusters, we employ two different methods, namely, the geometric characteristics of the space and an analysis of the agent's action distributions. Furthermore, we have introduced a visually assisted ranking algorithm leveraging pre-trained convolutional neural networks. The efficacy of our method has been demonstrated on two diverse reward spaces, which we have successfully adapted for navigating two distinct 2D platforms: a virtual kitchen and an off-road terrain.

We're exploring nucleon structure functions within noncommutative space-time, with the aim of uncovering the internal makeup of nucleons. To do this, we're utilizing corrected and novel vertices that arise from noncommutativity, and we're expressing the proton's structure functions using the noncommutative tensor \theta_{\mu\nu}. Our results are verified by comparing the calculated nucleon structure function (F_2(x)) to both experimental data and predictions from GRV, GJR, and CT10 models. Importantly, our noncommutativity-corrected structure functions reveal a more nuanced, complex picture of nucleon composition. We're also investigating the impact of noncommutativity on nucleon mass. To this end, we're calculating the nucleon's mass correction as a function of θ^2, which turns out to be proportional to θ^2. However, these corrections are significantly smaller than the nucleon's overall mass.

In typical topological systems, significant disruptions trigger a phase shift, but we have developed an adjustable version of the Toric code that remains stable under even extreme external influences, characterized by a "critical line" where no phase shift occurs, and exhibits gradual changes in behavior along this threshold. This theoretical model can be successfully implemented in laboratory settings using a 2D grid of qubits and specially designed anisotropic interactions. Upon optimizing the interaction strengths, our theoretical and simulated results match the expected topological behavior, even though the "critical line" persists in randomly disrupted systems, it distinguishes our model from standard topological systems, which tend to undergo phase shifts at relatively minor disturbances.

We investigate the eigenspectra of large, randomly constructed Hermitian block matrices, whose structure is perturbed by a finite rank complex modification. Given that the band's width expands faster than the square root of the matrix's size, our analysis demonstrates that the statistical distribution of the imaginary components of the eigenvectors aligns with the results from the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. This finding was achieved using the methods and approaches developed in the arXiv paper, 1802.03813.

Recent advancements in dialogue tasks like empathy and sentiment analysis have been achieved through dialogue pre-training with unsupervised objectives. This paper presents an alternative approach that takes into account the rich semantics of dialogue from the start. It combines a BERT-based model for dialogue with pre-training tasks that reflect the meaning of the spoken words and the structure of dialogue conversations. The proposed pre-training strategy is evaluated on NDS, a benchmark for natural dialogue understanding that measures the ability to convey empathy, understand the feelings and intentions of others, and recall relevant dialogue context. The results show that this pre-training strategy is more effective at improving dialogue understanding skills than previous methods that relied solely on dialogue sequence-based pre-training. Furthermore, the study finds that incorporating dialogue structure and semantics-based pre-training can also aid in the development of more empathetic dialogue systems.

To assess the requirements for an intelligent system to learn and apply its knowledge, we developed a theoretical framework for algorithmic interpretability. This framework consists of three key components: the algorithm's knowledge, its understanding of that knowledge, and its ability to convey that understanding to others. We applied this framework to a large batch of algorithms, evaluating their fundamental complexity based on both human mathematical and general cognitive perspectives. The results showed that deeper understanding and broader cognitive bases often correlate with increased algorithmic interpretability, as measured by a notable scale. The scale revealed that certain algorithms, such as those relying on symbolic reasoning, have a relatively low interpretability score, while those employing complex numerical methods have a relatively high one, with some attention-based models falling in between. The scale also distinguished between algorithms that communicate through visual representations, written descriptions, or a combination of both. The results highlighted the practical value of our framework, providing a basis for algorithms to be evaluated based on their capacity for transparent explanation and potential application in industry settings.

Anomaly detection without a guide can be a demanding and inflexible issue.
Typically, unsupervised anomaly detection methods are either unreliable or
require a significant number of instances with labels. This paper presents an
unsupervised anomaly detection approach that relies on a single, uncomplicated
data source without compromising detection precision. The proposed method
builds upon Isolation Forest, leveraging an innovative data augmentation
technique from the domain of weakly supervised learning to enhance its
performance. Furthermore, the proposed method can function effectively in
environments where storage and computational resources are limited. The
efficacy of this method is demonstrated through experiments on benchmark datasets
as well as scenarios involving real-world applications, showcasing its ability
to identify anomalies in images without manual labeling. The source code is
available online at the address https://github.com/AndreMSangueira/TiWS-iForest.

A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. In this paper, we employ a full Bayesian approach, combining prior knowledge of both the threshold exceedance rate and the Pareto index to quantify uncertainty in their estimates. A novel simulation-based technique, inspired by the time transformation approach, is developed to sample extremes from non-stationary, discrete time Poisson distributions, enabling Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling. A detailed description of this method, along with its application in a real-world scenario with data on significant rainfall in England, is presented.

This analysis addresses the issue of identifying stationary points in the average cross section, which describes the average scattering distribution when particles are distributed uniformly across an interval. The model is based on a simple differential equation with specified boundary conditions. By applying mathematical techniques, it is determined that stationary points must lie within a restricted range. A pivotal finding is the presence of a single stationary value, bounded by the minimum and maximum values of the interval in question. The existence of stationary values at interval endpoints is also confirmed, as well as their distinct nature in comparison to the central stationary value. The existence of stationary values at interval endpoints is also confirmed, with each having distinct magnitudes in comparison to the central one. The mathematical underpinning of this issue is also related to a broader concept in the field of scattering theory, specifically the phenomenon of bound state emergence.

The release of the COMET-ATOMIC dataset in 2020 marks a significant step in 
preparing data pipelines for commonsense knowledge representation and a wide 
range of downstream applications in computer vision and natural language 
processing. This update builds upon previous $2\times$ sized updates to bring 
the total number of atomic events to 13M, symbolically linked to over 118K 
syntactic predicates, and neutrally associated with 64K distributed word 
embeddings. The dataset is made publicly accessible through both a symbolic 
database and a neural knowledge graph, with instructions on how to access 
and use the data. Additionally, this update includes the selection of 64 
distributed word embeddings that effectively capture common sense concepts, 
and provides explanations for any potential discrepancies found during 
common sense reasoning operations. Finally, this update highlights potential 
use cases for the updated ATOMIC dataset.

We introduce the data processing pipeline developed for the Hi-GAL survey. This critical component is an integral part of the Herschel satellite project that's mapping the Galactic plane's inner regions. Leveraging a combination of Herschel Interactive Standard Environment capabilities and new, custom-designed tools, our pipeline effectively handles data reduction tasks. These include accurate data filtering, noise assessment, and efficient map generation, which utilizes a highly modified version of the HECA algorithm. Our work outlines the reduction pipeline's execution for Hi-GAL data, describing specific science calibration, map generation, and additional data analysis processes. These procedures properly handle the various science channels found in Herschel's Spectral and Nodal Project data. The resulting output includes calibrated data, a detailed noise model, and sophisticated maps generated using a highly efficient and accurate method. These processed data are further analyzed using additional tools, which include a novel implementation of the Moriond algorithm for spatial noise reduction, and deep learning models to classify dust morphology.

Recent studies of the globular cluster NGC 2808 uncovered initial composition discrepancies that raised questions about its possible multiple metal levels. Further research aimed to re-examine the composition using more precise methods and compare the compositions of various stars within the cluster. A specific technique was used to analyze the compositions of multiple stars with different brightness levels and spatial positions within the cluster. The results revealed higher metal levels in comparison to previous studies and a notable spread in metal levels within the cluster. A comparison of the compositions of multiple stars within the cluster also suggested the presence of two distinct stellar populations. These findings support previous theories of a complex star formation history within NGC 2808 and a possible interaction between these two stellar populations. In contrast to earlier assumptions, these two populations appear to coexist within the same geographic location within the cluster. A possible explanation for the observed spread in metal levels within the cluster is the presence of a relatively small number of more metal-rich stars within the cluster. These more metal-rich stars appear to be part of the second, younger population within the cluster. A specific model was used to analyze the distribution of these two distinct stellar populations within the cluster and support the presence of a metal-rich population within the cluster. This model also suggested that the initial composition of the second, younger population within the cluster was relatively high in helium. A specific value for the initial helium content within the second, younger population within the cluster was estimated. To facilitate a deeper understanding of one-dimensional physical systems, we consider a simplified single file model. We derive an analytical solution for the complete probability distribution of the first exit time from a defined interval in the single file model. This solution possesses universal characteristics, with its first moment matching the outcome from the central limit theorem. Furthermore, we obtain the entropic effective force acting on a particle located at $x$ in the single file model through the reverse engineering approach. The shape of the effective force is examined and compared under different scenario conditions. Notably, when the effective force is either at its maximum or minimum, it reveals the presence of singular characteristics; specifically, it displays an inverse relationship at its minimum, with the distance between the examined particle and the interval's end potentially approaching zero.

These findings also account for non-thermal considerations. We discovered that, up to the second order, the ratio of energy density to entropy density is largely independent of the system size, exhibiting minimal variations. Notably, even at the second order, significant system-size dependence exists for the pressure, viscosity, polymeric flow, and higher flow coefficients, encouraging further investigation. We outline the necessary approach to system size for its accurate correlation with temperature and relevant physical properties. We also present findings from preliminary microscopic calculations and compare them with similar data from perturbative QCD, showcasing significant system-size dependence in numerous physical properties. These findings suggest that continuing to the third order will not eliminate system-size dependence. Let $F_2$ be the prime field consisting of two elements. The general linear group of rank $s$, denoted as $GL_s$, represents the general linear group of degree $s$ over $F_2$. The Steenrod algebra $\mathcal A$ can be expressed as a subalgebra within the graded coordinate ring of $GL_s$. In this context, we are concerned with the $\mathcal A$-cohomology groups of the degree $-s$, denoted as $\mathcal A^*(-s)$. The $\mathcal A$-cohomology groups of the degree $-s$ contain an element of degree $2s$ that is known as the 'transverse invariant'. This element is an autoinvariant element of the degree $2s$. The 'transverse invariant' can be represented by the product of the mod $2$ Wu classes and Steenrod squares in the cohomology groups of the complex projective space. The degree-$2s$ element of the $\mathcal A$-cohomology groups of the degree $-s$ also possesses a property known as 'nilpotent up to action by $\mathcal A$'.

Astronomers observing far ultraviolet wavelengths from space have been restricted by interstellar hydrogen's Lyman-alpha radiation, despite offering critical insights into high-energy events like star formation and quasars. A Lyman-alpha filter, previously developed for land-based telescopes, has enabled transmission of this radiation by filtering out its most prominent wavelength. As technology advances and space-based telescopes' wavelengths expand, a new LAF was designed to support increasingly capable UV space telescopes, boasting superior performance and set to revolutionize the field with its first application on the James Webb Space Telescope.

Optimal controller design under graph filtering constraints can be complex and
sensitive to filtering limitations in large graph systems. This paper presents a
networked control approach that leverages graph filter theories and distributed
control theories to overcome these challenges in optimal controller design.
Specifically, we derive a decentralized algorithm for designing optimal control
inputs, which efficiently operates within the graph network without requiring
global system information. This approach utilizes node-level summation and
prediction capabilities from the graph filter framework, similar to Subgradient
Method, to converge towards an optimal solution under certain conditions. We
test this innovative method using a node velocity control problem on a
swarm of robots to demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency in the
real-world application.

Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from large databases comprise two main components: a neural network that converts an image into a transformation-resistant vector, and a high-performance but imperfect search algorithm. This paper introduces active indexing to optimize the interplay between these components, reducing a representation's loss through subtle, imperceptible modifications to images before their release. Our modifications enhance the image's retrievability, with backpropagation of the loss through the transformation layer, and are validated across various extraction techniques and databases, resulting in a notable improvement in retrieval precision, with up to a 40% increase in our experiments.

This study confirms that physical layer-based authentication is achievable in
Gaussian noise environments, with the caveat that an all-knowing adversary cannot be
beated. An examination of a model comprising encoder, decoder, and adversary was
carried out, with the constraint that an eavesdropping device must remain anonymous.
For this model, an information theoretic limit on error rate in authentication was
first established under any legitimate communication scheme, then again when the
transmitter knows the encryption method. When the number of transmissions is large,
these two limits were found to be practically the same. Finally, the study considered
the capacity for secure communication in this model and found it to be very similar
to that established for authentication.

Reevaluating the "dispersionless transport regime" of Brownian particles in inclined periodic potentials, we found that after entering a running state under the influence of a constant force, these particles display typical diffusive behavior without experiencing unique transient dynamics as previously hypothesized. The flat section in the dispersion evolution curve can be entirely attributed to the particles' wide spatial distribution resulting from an earlier stage of superdiffusion, which eventually transitions to normal diffusion as the particles' spatial spread diminishes. The rates of spatial spreading can be calculated using a novel method combining the two-point probability function and the power spectral density, thereby offering a more accurate picture of transport dynamics in washboard potentials. The findings are equally applicable to other systems featuring overdamped motion, such as charge dynamics in superlattices under bias voltage.

This paper presents an adaptable, localized predictive technique that builds upon Jord\'a's (2005) model, expanding it to a non-statistical setting through the incorporation of Bayesian Additive Regression Trees. Simulation tests reveal that our novel BART-LP model successfully captures the complexities present in the impact responses of various shocks. Case studies on the consequences of U.S. tax policy changes and the effects of high-frequency financial volatility are provided to demonstrate the efficacy of the model.

We investigate the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum on the angular momentum of a charge q moving in a uniform magnetic field. The orbital angular momentum generated is due to the charge's interaction with photons in the quantum vacuum, induced by the Landau level splitting experienced by the charge. The total orbital angular momentum exhibited by the charge or the magnetic field alone reaches the quantum limit, displaying a discrete, quantized quality.

The primary goal of Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) is to identify
precise entity types from a comprehensive taxonomy, often containing numerous
subcategories. Traditional FG-NET approaches suffer from limitations, such as
the efficiency problem (slowing performance with taxonomy scale) and the
coverage problem (struggling to recognize entity types entirely absent from the taxonomy). To address these challenges, this study introduces FGNET-RH, a innovative end-to-end model that utilizes the hyperbolic embedding technique to efficiently train accurate entity type representations for extensive and complex taxonomy scales. FGNET-RH specifically comprises two key components: a head entity extractor that initially identifies dominant entity types and a hyperbolic refinement module refining these representations through a soft matching process. By incorporating a hyperbolic loss function, FGNET-RH achieves significant improvements over alternative approaches, ultimately resulting in higher micro-F1 scores for the 143D dataset. Furthermore, the integration of a new type pointer into the FGNET-RH architecture enables effective coverage of entity types absent from the taxonomy, ultimately resulting in improved performance on the domain adaptation dataset TAC KB.

This paper establishes upper limits on the Hankel determinants for the $H_2(3)(f)$ and $H_2(4)(f)$ special types, specifically within the univalent function class and the $\mathcal{U}$ class defined by a specific condition involving functions that are analytic in the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$, with normalization where $f(z)=z+a_2z^2+\cdots$.

Achieving efficient and sustainable operation in cloud data centers largely relies on load balancing, and the placement of virtual machines plays a crucial role in achieving optimal performance. The placement issue is complex due to the interconnected nature of VMs, which reduces the applicability of traditional strategies. This paper proposes Prepartition, a novel load balancing approach for achieving stable output and fast run times in conjunction with a monolithic architecture that utilizes cut-and-pack. The evaluation of Prepartition demonstrates significant improvements over current methodologies, yielding up to a 50-fold reduction in computation time and a 2-fold decrease in output variability compared to the time-progressive cut-and-join method and time-regressive Round Robin strategy.

In modeling systems of rival agents as games, equilibrium concepts like Nash equilibrium significantly influence the study of their behavior. This research proposes the fixed point network (FPN), a novel neural network designed to learn various equilibrium types, by utilizing a fixed point perspective. FPN incorporates the Banach fixed point theorem, providing a mathematical framework for its training and assessment. It exploits the universal approximation properties of multilayer perceptrons to represent general fixed-point problems. Through experiments, FPN demonstrates superior performance in predicting both Nash equilibrium and evolutionarily stable states. It also shows its ability to extend its findings from a simplified 2-D setting to more complex scenarios, including 10-D games and various types of Nash equilibrium.

This study tackles the issue of assessing causal influences in cases where some variables involved in ensuring causal validity are incompletely known. For these situations, we develop tight limits on the causal influences by solving two intricate optimization problems. The derived limits prove to be sufficient, leading us to introduce an optimization technique, enabling dimensionality reduction that can specifically address data with high dimensions, ultimately facilitating generalizable conclusions. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through a series of simulated experiments and real-world data analysis.

Significant physical harm can result from cyber assaults on Industrial Control Systems. Although in-person assessments can reveal vulnerable system components, they may not be effective against covert attacks that bypass detection during prolonged operations. We present a predictive real-time monitoring method in this study to identify whether a Linear Time-Invariant system's behavior within a given timeframe is consistent with expected, undisturbed system behavior. This expectation is based on prior, uncomplicated system data. Our proposal combines established spectral techniques with contemporary attack simulation concepts to make predictions based on limited, pre-attack system data more reliable and efficient. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness on a model of the IEEE Phase II Benchmarks and further investigate its operation.

A precise summary can be derived from lengthy written documents via deep learning models, but English language models often benefit from larger training sets and pre-trained tools, whereas summarization for lesser-known Indian languages is hindered by complex syntax and differences in word order and meaning. A solution to this issue is presented in the form of GAE-ISumm: a universal graph-based model utilizing a simple yet efficient representation that can effectively create informative summaries for these languages despite their differences. Furthermore, GAE-ISumm has the potential to also enhance English language summarization performance.

We establish the definition and certain attributes of S-rings of Krull type, in addition to examining the properties of such structures, particularly independent S-rings of type A. We calculate the injective dimension of a quotient category formed by modules over an independent S-ring of type A, with respect to a subcategory consisting of modules having trivial interactions with the series of local primes less than or equal to n.

The objective of this research was to identify and characterise substellar companions and white dwarf companions that may be contributing to the unexpected motion in nearby late-type stars by conducting a thorough examination of two key radial velocity parameters. We conducted an in-depth analysis, combining existing data with time-series photometry and linear regression models to explore the physical properties of companion stars and their kinematic behavior. Five late-type stars were selected for the study: HIP 87937, HIP 88451, HIP 91617, HIP 94244, and HIP 104226. Radial velocity time-series data for these stars were also collected and analysed. However, no conclusive evidence of accelerating stars like Polux, Rho$^\dagger$ Bootis A, or eclipsing binary white dwarf companions was found in the systems. We developed models to explore the possible mass and separation ranges for unseen companions, but no specific candidate emerged to fully explain the unusual motion in the stars. The study provided constraints for potential companion masses and separations in the systems of HIP 91617 and HIP 94244, with the results suggesting a high likelihood of a low-mass companion in the latter, potentially an eclipsing white dwarf companion. Recent advances in variational Bayesian methods for neural networks have provided a practical solution for Bayesian inference, and recently improved variational approximations in Bayesian neural networks have facilitated fast and reliable approximations of uncertainty measures. Meanwhile, Bayesian inference in more complex structured models embedded within least square objective functions has been largely overlooked. This study addresses this gap by adapting the variational Bayesian approach to Bayesian neural networks optimized using least square objectives, and proposes a novel vae framework, including the derivation of the reparameterization technique for sampling. Furthermore, we investigate the applicability of posterior regularizations, and show that incorporating L1 and Dirichlet priors in the Bayesian neural network's latent space yields superior generalization performance. Results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach on synthetic and real-world data, and specifically the regression of human brain images from MRI.

Smart home technology is gaining momentum, driven by IoT, yet it also invites cyber threats that necessitate robust and intelligent security systems. This research contributes to this need by designing an IoT smart home security system that combines private blockchain technology, device tracking through the IPv6 protocol, and intrusion detection. The proposed system employs a private blockchain to record secure IoT data, including location information and unique device IDs embedded in IoT devices. The IPv6 protocol is used to track smart home devices by integrating it with the private blockchain for added security. The research includes experimental validation to demonstrate the effectiveness and advantages of this innovative solution.

A novel approach to quantizing log-likelihood ratio storage utilizing deep learning is presented. It was discovered that average L-values of QAM symbols exhibit a systematic pattern, making them amenable to a deep autoencoder representation. This allows for symmetric, power-limited distortion to be imposed on the encoder during training. In contrast to traditional lossy compression methods like source coding and quantization, this approach yields significantly improved results, with notable performance seen in extensions such as partial channel state information, multiple user scenarios, and even nonmemory-hierarchical structures.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. These findings were initially discovered in 2014 but are now presented in a more concise and structured format. We've also introduced a novel characterization for a specific type of planar layout known as strong upward planarity. Additionally, we've successfully developed a fixed-parameter algorithm in collaboration with S. Abrahao to identify whether a graph can be represented in a strong upward planar layout when the number of strong sources is taken into consideration as a parameter. This algorithm is also fixed-parameter with respect to the remaining strong sources. We've further extended this investigation to examine the parameterized complexity of the strong upward planarity problem when the focus is on the total number of strong sources instead. We've discovered that the problem does not have a polynomial-time algorithm unless a specific hypothesis is false. We've also proposed an alternative version of strong upward planarity known as $\omega$-strong upward planarity. We've demonstrated that the $\omega$-strong upward planarity problem is substantially more complex than its counterpart planarity problems when considering parameterized complexity. Crowdsourced image datasets, often marred by noise, pose a significant challenge for even the most sophisticated neural networks. This difficulty arises from class imbalance, inconsistent labeling, and partial information about the class assignments. A novel crowdsourced estimation technique has been developed to address these issues by leveraging ensemble modeling and incorporating measures of entropy to quantify uncertainty in dataset annotations. This approach relies on the application of Bayesian decision rules, softening the output class distributions ('human softmax') of pre-trained networks to facilitate reliable annotation predictions. The method utilizes maximum entropy principles and relies on the alpha-divergence measure for data regularization. The approach demonstrates a substantial improvement in annotation quality, surpassing existing methods by approximately 4.4% to 11.4% in terms of accuracy. The technique also relies on pre-trained neural networks, a criterion shared with previous methods such as TeamStat. However, the proposed approach eschews the use of voting algorithms, instead relying on the analysis of 'human softmax' distributions for annotation estimates. This technique has the added benefit of providing confidence intervals for individual and group annotation labels. The annotation quality was evaluated using inter-rater reliability metrics such as the mean and median
$\eta$-values. The proposed approach was tested on the two widely used ImageNet-Architecture datasets, namely Clothing Parts Dataset (CPD) and the DeepFashion Dataset. The results demonstrate the efficacy of the approach in handling datasets characterized by class imbalance, noisy annotations, and partial information about the class

For semiflows with uniformly or nonuniformly expanding dynamics, which exhibit exponential decay in correlations, we can prove the exponential decay in the H\"older norm of the transfer operators acting on smooth observables.

A particular matrix known as a covering array has specific characteristics. It is made up of different symbols and certain sub-matrices must include each combination of those symbols a set number of times. The best, or smallest, such matrices are known as optimal, and if they have uniform distribution of those symbols across all columns they're also referred to as uniform. Historically, optimal covering arrays of a certain size had been constructed in a particular way, however we provide an infinite number of examples where this construction method fails to be the most efficient.

This study verifies that a broad category of non-local games, involving imperfectly entangled pairs of quantum states, possess a clear and deterministic outcome. In practical terms, we demonstrate a device capable of accurately simulating any game involving such entangled pairs, regardless of how they were generated. We achieve this outcome without assuming the existence of a "black box" that generates ideal entangled pairs, but rather by assuming access to a device that can accurately produce approximately entangled pairs, with the level of accuracy depending on the specific game being tested. This finding expands upon a previous theory first proposed by Connes and Connes. We also explore a related issue, investigating under what conditions a game's outcome can be consistently predicted, given varying methods of approximating the entangled pairs, and show through an example involving random matrix theory that the predictability of the game's outcome can be consistently applied in certain game scenarios.

This study partially replicates the work by Soltani et al. who introduced EvoCrash, a novel open-source tool employing a guided genetic algorithm to automate software crash reproduction. By replicating the original results, this study confirms the efficacy of EvoCrash on multiple real-world applications. Notably, it also examines and contrasts EvoCrash's performance when applied to the JBoss ASP and Java 3D projects.

The quasiparticle spectrum observed under high-pressure, laser-excited Arctic melaniene-doped Bi-2201 is examined, and the resulting temperature-dependent anomalies are recorded. Notably, the observed spectrum exhibits a series of distinct minimum-energy peaks at specific integer multiples of a fundamental frequency, and these peaks undergo a sudden shift in frequency at critical temperatures of 35 and 38.5 degrees Fahrenheit for pressures of 24 and 28 thousand atmospheres, respectively. This frequency scaling phenomenon is consistent with the previously proposed model of square and square-pinwheel quasiparticle arrangements in cuprate superconductors, and the observed transitions are considered to be the result of the melting of square and square-pinwheel lattice structures.

Photons are valuable tools used to explore the intense medium produced in high-energy heavy-ion collisions. Recent research includes precise calculations of the influence of viscosity on photon emission in these collisions, taking place at RHIC and LHC. Thermal photons exhibit anisotropic movement patterns known as v_n coefficients, which are calculated considering and excluding viscosity effects. Surprisingly, the viscosity effects significantly impact these coefficients, more so than viscosity effects on overall movement patterns in the collision. Furthermore, the ratio of specific anisotropic movement patterns, such as v_2 and v_3, is highly sensitive to the viscosity of the quark-gluon plasma. As such, thermal photon anisotropic movement patterns offer a robust method for determining the viscosity of quark-gluon plasma.

Our study centers on investigating the regular magnetic order (RMO) for certain spin models with global spin rotations symmetries, focusing on group theoretical methods for triangular and kagome lattices. These regular magnetic orders hold significance as potential ground states for various spin models, making them prime candidates for study. By adhering to a framework developed by Messio et al., we extended their initial approach to incorporate specific subgroupings of the p6m symmetry group, such as p6, p3, p3m1, and p31m. For kagome and triangular lattices fitting these groupings, we have identified all corresponding regular magnetic orders. Calculations were then performed to determine the free energy of each state at zero temperature. Ultimately, our research includes a comparison of our results with existing literature on kagome and triangular spin models.

Large data-driven companies have considered online controlled experiments (A/B Testing) a gold standard for several decades. Many companies use a standard framework that measures "average treatment effect" (ATE), but there's a significant challenge to increase its detection power while maintaining "false discovery rate" (FDR) within a predetermined threshold. Popular algorithms like the BH method struggle to control FDR, particularly when encountering positive dependence, which requires conservative estimations. In this study, we propose an innovative newframe (i-newframe), which offers more efficient control over the FDR at a lower "false discovery proportion" (FDPro), thus enhancing detection power for the ATE. Compared to existing methods (BH and an improved version of LASER+), our results reveal that i-newframe offers 25-40% higher statistical power without any actual increase in FDR, and a 10-fold reduction in FDPro, demonstrating its superiority in more reliable detection of the ATE. Additionally, we showcase the efficacy of i-newframe in tackling real-world challenges from Google's search team.

The foundational aspects of cosmological inflation are addressed. The derivation of equations governing the inflaton field, an introduction to slow-roll parameters, and a description of how inflationary perturbations correspond to cosmic microwave background temperature fluctuations are presented.

The CDF II Collaboration has made a precise measurement of the W boson mass which deviates from the Standard Model's prediction by 7$\sigma$. The FNAL muon magnetic moment measurement also displays a $4.2\sigma$ discrepancy. In an effort to resolve the anomalies in the W boson and muon magnetic moments, we have investigated the type-X two Higgs doublet model. Our analysis focused on the type-X 2HDM's capacity to explain the observed differences within its parameter space, utilizing constraints on the muon $g-2$ anomaly along with the Higgs signal, di-boson, top quark production constraints, and the latest ATLAS and CDF II mass measurements for the W boson. We found that the type-X 2HDM can resolve the two anomalies concurrently for specific ranges of the scalar septet mass.

Software developers who perform maintenance tasks encounter multiple change requests 
submitted by software system users, each presenting the issue in question as part of 
their request description. For technical support staff to process these requests, 
they must transform the request into a query suitable for searching the system's source code, 
a task known as query reformulation. Research has shown that the majority of a developer's 
time is spent on performing maintenance tasks efficiently, including managing change requests. 
Although change management is a significant portion of a developer's workload, there 
has been little scientific investigation on how developers interact with such requests. 
Our research focuses on the challenge of reformulating user queries into suitable source code searches. 
We analyzed the content of a large dataset of user requests, identified their key characteristics, 
and collected crowd-sourced feedback to develop QUICKAR, an automatic query reformulation tool. 
Our study demonstrated the efficacy of QUICKAR through a comparative analysis with alternative methods.

Adaptive synchronization in interactions, or entrainment, involves the participants in a conversation adapting or matching each other's distinctive vocal characteristics to create a more harmonious interaction. The extent of adaptive synchronization has been shown to contribute to the development of social connections; for instance, research has found a connection between people adapting their speech patterns to each other and the formation of friendships. The existing measures of adaptive synchronization, however, have primarily been used in laboratory settings and studies of non-human primates, due in part to difficulties in processing complex voice data. A major breakthrough has been achieved in the processing of large amounts of vocal features using advanced machine learning techniques, which has created a need for an updated metric that can take advantage of these new methods. A key challenge in using modern machine learning techniques is the development of labels on a large scale, particularly in social interactions, which makes unsupervised learning an attractive option. A study has been conducted to assess the effectiveness of an unsupervised metric, or measure, of adaptive synchronization using a vast database of conversations and spoken words. The researchers compared multiple approaches, including the analysis of distinct voice patterns and different methods of leveraging advanced machine learning techniques. The study found that one specific approach, or model, performed better than others and was more accurate than a previous measure of adaptive synchronization. The effectiveness of this approach was confirmed through its alignment with established indicators of adaptive synchronization.
