Researchers have been exploring a groundbreaking laser-plasma platform for fundamental physics research, leveraging a high-powered laser that interacts with a plasmoid at ultra-high energy levels. This innovative setup has enabled the creation of a 20 cm long plasma lab for experimental and theoretical investigation into photon-photon collision experiments. Achieving a stable interaction requires precise control over laser and plasmoid characteristics as well as an understanding of the complex physical processes involved. This study describes the development of such a laser-plasma system and outlines the challenges associated with its implementation, while casting an eye on future research opportunities presented by this innovative platform.

In a forthcoming letter, we examine how sensitive the Two Higgs Doublet Model is to a crucial parameter, $m_{12}$, which breaks the symmetry softly and impacts the Higgs boson decays significantly. Along with other vital model parameters like tangent of the Higgs mixing angle and the ratio of Yukawa couplings, we perform a comprehensive study to determine the lower bounds $m_{12}$ can reach, all while keeping the mass of the second Higgs boson under 450 GeV and adhering to constraints from tree-level approximate percent level precision on Higgs boson decays.

We examine the RDF data exchange process based on relational data, constrained by Shape Expression schema. In contrast to previous work mainly focusing on basic data exchange, our research considers inclusion constraints and also explores the complexity of computing optimal primary key shapes in the target schema. Our analysis reveals that assessing isryptability for basic inclusion constraints, when the source schema includes various shapes, has a complexity of PTIME. Additionally, computing optimal primary key shapes can be achieved in EXPTIME. Furthermore, in the context of weak inclusion constraints, this process can be accomplished in 2EXPTIME. Our research further demonstrates that weak inclusion constraints increase data exchange complexity to at least 2EXPTIME, contrasting with the 3EXPTIME required for strong inclusion constraints.

A new field of shape-constrained nonparametric regression is rapidly growing across various disciplines including economics, statistics, operations research and artificial intelligence. Recent advancements in the analysis of productivity and efficiency now bridge a significant knowledge gap in this field. The application of these techniques yield highly interpretable results in a manageable number of dimensions. The implementation of several novel methods in the form of efficient and well-documented algorithms available within the open-source pyStoNED package serves as a significant contribution to the statistical community. The package provides a significant enhancement as it offers a significant reduction in computational costs coupled with increased accessibility for researchers. The pyStoNED package features a significant expansion of standalone algorithms for shape-constrained nonparametric regression and is available under an open-source license. The necessary instructions for installation and usage can be found on the package's official GitHub repository, located at https://github.com/gradet/pyStoNED.

This study proposes a novel strategy for searching the standard model's 125 GeV Higgs boson in conjunction with the top quark's partner, the heavy axially-coupled Higgs boson (aH), which has a mass less than 400 GeV and a significantly lighter 10-40 GeV Higgs boson (light Higgs, lH). In the analysis, an advanced single-ton approach is applied to the association of top quark pairs with the lH, utilizing the largest available dataset of LHC Run 2 data. Notably, this investigation reveals that the standard model's lH production via top quark pairs exhibits a more favorable sensitivity than production in association with a gluon, especially when the latter's coupling is used as a reference point.

Pre-trained language models possess a built-in grammar understanding, allowing them to generate coherent parse trees for given sentences without needing to be specifically trained for this task. We explore two methods to leverage this capability for grammar-based parsing. First, an unsupervised approach trains a transformer model on an ordered sequence of grammar rules and the corresponding sentence, using a log-linear model with various features to determine the top-most rule. This method produces promising results on the Penn Treebank, equal to or matching the performance of similar models in unsupervised parsing. Additionally, we adapt this method to work with a pre-trained language model in a sequence-to-sequence transformer parsing framework, achieving comparable performance on the same dataset. We also present a few-shot learning experiment where the model is trained on a small corpus from another source, and then applied to the CoNLL-2005 English dataset, achieving a relatively high performance for unsupervised parsing on this dataset.

The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on high-quality Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). Despite having access to advanced ASR tools, the support for lesser spoken languages remains limited. This shortage is particularly pronounced in languages with limited resources such as German dialects like Lower Saxon, characterized by slight variations in pronunciation, resulting in significant differences with Standard German. This issue leads to significant errors in ASR, causing obstacles for users who primarily interact in dialects. A recently developed open-source German ASR model named KSPN-16T has demonstrated exceptional performance, achieving a high mark of 93.16% in terms of word accuracy on the LibriSpeech-960 corpus. This model, based on Kaldi and Keras, has shown remarkable performance and is highly adaptable to dialects. The integration of a data-driven pronunciation rule model further enhances accuracy, with a 3.5% improvement over a baseline model on a dialect-specific corpus.

The origin of Be-type stars is still unclear with theories involving both single and dual star evolutions, however through 73 VFTS spectra analyses it has been observed that Be-type stars have higher rotational speeds. Calculations reveal that their projected rotation speeds cannot all be at critical velocity as there are 37 Be-type stars with secondary orbits, showing rotational velocities ranging between 230 to 320 km/s. In contrast, the majority of single stars have rotation speeds at critical velocity or greater.

To translate ASR output into written text, inverse text normalization is used (ITN). Currently, ITN approaches rely on large datasets of written text paired with their spoken counterparts. However, this data shortcomings significantly hinder ITN performance due to a significant gap between spoken and written language. This problem is addressed by a novel data enhancement technique that synthesizes a larger, more diverse corpus from existing resources. When applied to a standard ITN assessment, our method demonstrated a notable 2.1 BLEU score increase over the baseline.

This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue 
of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, showing 
that the optimal configuration is a half-space, and investigates the conditions 
under which equality occurs.

Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, are often difficult to understand. This interpretability issue severely hampers their use in critical areas like medical imaging. A promising approach, neural tangent kernel, offers some level of interpretation by mirroring a kernel machine's properties. In this paper, we enhance the NTK model by combining it with non-fungible tangential kernels, resulting in NFTK-NTK. To our knowledge, we are the first to explore non-fungible kernels in the NTK framework. By exploring NK-NTK, we demonstrate that it retains key characteristics of both models, including its ability to attain global optima and avoid local minima through data augmentation. Unlike NT-NTK, NK-NTK also offers the capability of parameter regularization without sacrificing its ability to attain global optima. Moreover, NFTK-NTK models exhibit improved medical image classification performance compared to NT-NTK models, while maintaining comparable training and prediction speeds.

Despite numerous research on the topology of non-Hermitian systems, there is a scarcity of studies on correlated non-Hermitian systems. We investigate one-dimensional correlated systems with a non-Hermitian term, placing them into different topological categories - the exceptional point point-gap topology and the generalized band topology. The topological characteristics of these systems can be altered due to correlations, with correlations having no impact on systems possessing an exceptional point but affecting those without. The reductions of topological categories of correlated systems are experimentally applicable in light-matter systems through the adjustment of coupling strengths. The topological characteristics of correlated systems can also be identified through the evaluation of correlation effects in quasi-particle spectra, with distinct topological categories being represented by specific distribution functions. The topological features of correlated systems can be quantitatively assessed using the intrinsic linking number of quasi-particle spectra. The implications of correlations on the topological characteristics of correlated systems can be explored through the correlation effects in systems of coupled bosons and fermions. The findings of this study demonstrate the potential interactions in correlated systems to modify their topological characteristics.

Our current research builds upon our earlier findings where we identified acoustic characteristics essential to synthetic speech perception as warm and competent. We now aim to explore how these derived vocal attributes contribute to their creation in the desired characteristics. We've specifically examined the potential of spectral flux, F1 mean, F2 mean, and their combinations in fostering warmth in female speech and the impact of voiced slope, spectral flux, and their combinations in projecting competence in female speech within synthetic voices. We've successfully integrated a feature quantization system into the standard Tacotron2 framework, and the results indicate that combining perceived attributes with conventional acoustics produces more accurate ratings of warmth and competence in human listeners.

A radiative seesaw model incorporating light dark matter and featuring modular A4 and gauged U(1)_(B-L) symmetries is proposed, where neutrino masses are produced through one-loop interactions, resulting in a bosonic dark matter candidate within the range of approximately 0.01-50 GeV. Stochastic Gradient Descent is employed to determine the best-fitting parameter set for neutrino properties, such as oscillation frequencies and mixing angles. Considering the most used neutrino frequency datasets from double chain reactions, we explore various cosmological constraints on dark matter such as X-ray observations, relic density, and direct detection experiments, and find suitable model options capable of fitting all conditions.

Building on the Heisenberg algebra concept of minimal length, a new geometrical approach to the Bohr-Mottelson model for nuclei is explored. By combining deformed canonical commutation relations with the Runge-Lenz vector, a quadrupole collective Hamiltonian operator is formulated. In the course of developing this operator, a computationally feasible solution is sought via a straightforward extension of the Schrodinger equation, resulting in eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. In turn, these solutions are utilized to construct eigenfunctions of the collective angular momentum operator. Numerical investigations are conducted on $^{156}$Gd and $^{820}$Hg isotopes to assess the minimal length effect's influence on eigenenergies, spectra widths, and eigenfunctions. In addition, the minimal length parameter's optimal value is identified by minimizing the average or expectation width of the spectral eigenvalues, thereby providing further insight into the quasiparticle deformation.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible on any GCM with ring identities that have distinct squares, and GCA quadruples are possible on GCMs with ring identities featuring four distinct squares in each pair.

Incorporating dimensionality reduction techniques, researchers address the complexities of analyzing numerous spectral bands within bi-temporal hyperspectral images. This study proposes a cutting-edge approach using a novel deep convolutional autoencoder that fuses features across hierarchical levels and receptive fields. By utilizing an unsupervised change detection technique, it overcomes the limitations of other label-dependent methods. By evaluating various configurations of sparse and feature fusion autoencoders on diverse hyperspectral datasets, it demonstrates the effectiveness of this innovative method across different parameter settings and image domains.

A comprehensive study examines the connection between residual entropy and viscosity using an extensive, high-accuracy dataset. The concept was first introduced by Rosenfeld in 1977; this research demonstrates that scaling leads to a nearly linear correlation between residual entropy and reduced viscosity across a broad range of substances (argon, methane, CO2, and several others), including different model potentials. The initial "universal" correlation of Rosenfeld was found to be limited, yet adjusting the density can successfully relate the viscosity of non-associated fluids to idealized models. Consequently, this comparison generates a length that directly relates to the liquid's cubic root volume.

The possibility that our Universe is embedded in a vast, flat space with negative curvature is intriguing, which would make it possible for the curvature to be perceived as an internal dark energy component driving the current expansion. Periodic cosmology has the added benefit of providing a natural explanation for the coherence of CMB, which would otherwise be expected to decay due to the phenomenon of gravitational Rayleigh-Taylor instability. In this study, we thoroughly examine the theoretical foundations of periodic cosmology, which necessitates a specific type of space-time geometry that forms closed curves in 3D. We derive essential equations for this scenario and proceed to calculate the redshift of photons, the number of neutrino species, and the curvature radius. Furthermore, we investigate key observational constraints on the model parameters, which include the curvature radius and Hubble scale, which are estimated to be approximately $120\%$ and $75\%$ larger than their standard values, respectively. The model is also consistent with the estimated age of the Universe if the curvature radius is sufficiently large.

A new superdeterministic theory of quantum mechanics known as Invariant-set theory is being proposed. This idea brings concepts from areas like chaos theory and dynamical systems into the study of quantum foundations. Despite some claims about the theory's strength, concerning its ability to resolve the quantum vs. reality debate, flaws have been found in one of its key mathematical foundations. This issue lies within a main theorem which relies on a fundamental concept but fails to provide an adequate definition for it. In addition, there are also issues with regard to the theory's nomological interpretation. In an attempt to rectify the theory, a hidden-variable framework has been implemented for Invariant-set theory. This has led to the discovery of further problems with the theory. Issues with the theory's mathematical foundations are similar to those found in the original hidden-variable framework. This analysis also explores how the theory can be compared to other quantum foundations proposals.

We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting on devices such as smart speakers and wearables. Our focus is on NN execution within IoT devices, which poses limitations in terms of processing power, memory, and energy consumption. To address these constraints, NNs are typically trained on embedded real-life speech datasets, employing a time-downsampling technique to decrease data resolution. This technique concurrent reduction of: data quantity, data feature richness, and input sequence length. It enables training of more robust NNs that can tolerate these factors and still recognize keywords. Following the training, various architectures are evaluated for their performance in keyword spotting, using an F-score metric that balances false positives and false negatives. Notably, the best F-score achieved is approximately 0.91, which occurs when the data resolution is reduced to one-sixth during testing. Additionally, the optimal F-score occurs at a point where the NN model complexity is relatively low. Our study employs the RECOLA dataset, which is specifically tailored for voice assistant applications.

In the case where lattice spacing vanishes, the analysis focuses on the dimer model on isoradial graphs in the presence of $SL(N,\mathbb{C})$ gauge fields with zero curl except for isolated singularities. It is known that on the conformal phase, the dimer model's partition function reflects the volume of an $SL(N,\mathbb{C})$ character locus. Notably, in this scenario, the model's ground states correspond to the zero-ordinate component of Dirac wave functions in the aforementioned gauge fields. Consequently, in the course of taking the limit where lattice spacing approaches zero, the wave functions' discrete spectrum gets absorbed into the gauge field's singularities, signifying a transformation from the $SL(N,\mathbb{C})$ representation space to $\mathbb{C}^N$ except at points of non-zero curl. The analysis extends to the Kasteleyn-Kadanoff inversions, the face-centered dimer model, and $SO(N,\mathbb{C})$ by allowing for an orthonormal framing on the graph, which leads to the emergence of zero modes corresponding to the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ vorticity in the gauge field's curl's homotopy group when $N$ equals two.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size.

In recent years, the needs of embedded systems have grown more complex.  These systems not only require reliable, hard real-time capabilities but also diverse functions such as network capabilities, 3D graphics, and trusted execution.  Implementing all the required features in a single chip is impractical because it would necessitate developing and testing new firmware,  and then integrating it with the existing code, which is time-consuming and error-prone.  Additionally, incorporating virtualization support into existing embedded systems is unattractive because it necessitates a hypervisor, which reduces the real-time performance and introduces new latency.  However, the primary embedding of the hypervisor within the hardware offers a range of benefits, which could offset the potential drawbacks.  In this research, we propose a plan to embed the hypervisor into the hardware, which would allow the hypervisor to take advantage of the system's hardware capabilities.  Our proposal aims to achieve a hypervisor with minimal overhead, which could be realized by embedding the hypervisor within the hardware.  We analyzed the hypervisor architecture and identified key design considerations and the trade-offs associated with each, which could guide the design of the hardware-integrated hypervisor.  Finally, we proposed T-Visor, which is a hypervisor architecture designed for mixed criticality embedded real-time systems.  Our evaluation showed that T-Visor has the potential to offer a high level of real-time performance, which could approach the native system performance, which is an

When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals typically align their camera lenses parallel to the ground to avoid complex perspective issues. Building upon this fundamental principle, many current stitching algorithms struggle to account for varying focal lengths or significant tilts from the initial orientation. To address this challenge, we focus on creating minimal solutions for optimal alignment and positioning of multiple images, given that they are oriented vertically, with unknown tilt angles accounted for through a single variable representing the entire scene's perspective convergence. By integrating key features like image scale, vanishing points, and the entrance points where lines converge, the proposed method significantly enhances simplicity and functionality by avoiding traditional perspective hacking techniques, thus making it suitable for various image scaling scenarios and tilts from the standard orientation. The presented approach also scales efficiently with increasing image counts and utilizes open-source tools like OpenCV for some components, in addition to providing near-minimal solutions for tilt angles by applying singular value decomposition to a matrix of linear equations. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through new, uncalibrated capture techniques that defy traditional perspective norms, featuring extreme camera tilt angles and varying focal lengths.

Chimeras are particular types of oscillatory networks where a subset of elements create artificial rhythms apart from the rest of the system. In this study, we explore chimeras in coupled phase oscillators with heterogeneous frequencies that are uniformly distributed within a system. We start with a basic model and then expand it by introducing an alpha fraction of Watanabe-Strogatz coupling and observe chimeras in both cases. Interestingly, as the alpha fraction increases, the size of the chimeric branch decreases, but it still exists when exclusive monotonic coupling is present. We also identify steady points and evaluate how system parameters influence their stability.

We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust and adaptable when dealing with slight environmental variations. Building upon the concept from PILCO, a method for probabilistic policy search, our research demonstrates that constraining the uncertainty in the Gaussian Process model's dynamics has a beneficial effect on policy updates and results in more resilient controllers. In addition, our findings highlight the practical advantages of this approach in a simulated robotic task.

We reinterpret Miller and Vial's slice algebras by replacing row vectors with multi-layer quivers, allowing for more nuanced representations. By generalizing preprojective algebras from paths to multi-layer quivers, we discover new classes of algebras, distinct from Miller and Vial's construction. Notably, when a path quiver is replaced with a star quiver, the resulting algebra undergoes a transformation similar to taking the higher power algebras of the original.

Research in holographic theories reveals a duality between reflected entropy and entanglement wedge cross-sectional area.  Building upon this concept, a similar duality is demonstrated using random tensor networks.  By examining individual tensors, non-trivial effects are discovered that resolve discrepancies at the page phase transition.  By aggregating these effects, the reflected entropy model is reestablished and enhanced.  Furthermore, this approach yields a novel, more comprehensive model for entropy, encompassing both term and tensor contributions.  It aligns with holographic duality and goes beyond it by providing a non-geometric, network-based explanation.

Understanding heritable information in unpredictable systems is essential for 
explanation and prediction in biology. We develop a framework to assess the 
measurable heritable information that flows from parents to offspring in 
stochastic evolution models. This framework aligns with the definition of 
heritable information even in systems lacking time-scale separability, 
independent of specific implementation details. Furthermore, this concept 
can also describe information transmission in electronic circuits with multiple 
components. Moreover, electronic circuits with multiple time scales offer a 
testbed for testing our theoretical framework. We utilize a biological 
evolution model, based on the theory of multi-scale time evolution, to show 
how the theoretical measures of heritable information decrease exponentially with 
time, starting from the initial conditions. However, if an unpredictable system 
has distinct separation of time scales, where the slower process is highly 
correlated with the faster process, we show that the heritable information 
decreases exponentially with time, starting from the initial conditions, 
influenced by the specific time scales. We also derive the heritable information 
in an unbiased electronic circuit model characterized by multi-scale time 
evolution, where the theoretical measures of heritable information decrease 
exponentially with time, starting from the initial conditions.

We investigate the dynamics of a basic 3D version of the H\'{e}non map, specifically focusing on its dissipative and orientation-preserving variants. A thorough analysis of bifurcations in this system reveals that the emergence of periodic orbits, especially at specific resonant points, leads to distinct patterns in the parameter space. The system also exhibits complex attractors such as invariant circles and chaotic motion, identifiable through rotation numbers and Lyapunov exponents. The chaotic motion includes patterns similar to those of H\'{e}non and Lorenz systems, arising either from a period-doubling sequence or from the disruption of stable circles near the unstable trajectory of a fixed point.

The gravitational-gauge theory relationship known as the double copy is a well established concept that links both scattering amplitudes and classical solutions, as well as suggesting its application to more complex, non-perturbative data. This study investigates the characteristics of manifolds in the gravitational field by proposing an alternative version of the double copy theory with a singular approach to gravitational properties distinct from gauge theories. It presents specific instances where the singular approach can be simplified and highlights its potential utility in further expanding the double copy theory, while also addressing and rectifying previous inaccuracies in the field regarding Wilson lines and gravitational properties.

We analyze the statistical behavior for specific $t = 2$ or $3$, examining how
the number of hook lengths divisible by $t$ in the partitions of $n$ varies.
The support of the resulting distribution, $Y_t(n)$, diminishes significantly
as $n$ becomes large, confirming a conjecture made by R. Caprino, R. Donagi and
C. Massone. Additionally, data collected from Mehta and Rains' study on the
probability density functions and cumulative distribution functions of $Y_2(n)$
and $Y_3(n)$ show that these distributions converge towards a specific point
mass. The study also derives the mean, variance and higher moments of these
distributions. The study further reveals that the number of Young tableaux with
hook lengths all divisible by two or three has a geometric distribution.

Quantum systems exhibit distinct behavior when passing through potential barriers,
distinguishing themselves from classical systems with a defined trajectory.
Tunneling time is a crucial parameter characterizing this quantum phenomenon.
It's noteworthy that tunneling time isn't just relevant to particles with specific spin,
but also influences the accuracy of spin-flipped clocks. Such clocks, relying on Larmor
rotation to measure time, can be impacted by the tunneling time of the spinning electron.
Although initially disregarded in time measurement discussions, this electron tunneling
phenomenon has implications for clock precision. Studies of ferromagnetic surfaces,
with their exchange field, have further implications for spin-flipped time measurement.
Considerations of tunneling time have led to the prediction of an inherent clock error,
resulting in lengthened time measurements. This error arises from particle tunneling,
potentially linked to superconductivity and the quantum coherence of second-order terms.
Its study may also shed light on the quantum system's unique particle-tunneling time,
involving virtual particles and the complex phenomenon of tunneling.

This research calculates the leading twist distribution amplitudes for P-wave non-relativistic mesons, building upon the existing theory of light-cone sum rules and the spin-1 light-cone sum rules framework. Essential to this process are the principles of non-relativistic heavy quark effective theory and the application of the Isgur-Wise form factor. The calculated amplitudes, expressed as a function of the non-relativistic parameter $m/\bar m$, display significant model dependence. Our model, drawing upon the light-front formalism, yields the amplitudes $\mathcal{A}^{(1)}(0)$ and $\mathcal{A}^{(8)}(0)$, while the asymptotic models establish the amplitudes $\mathcal{A}^{(1)}_{\infty}$ and $\mathcal{A}^{(8)}_{\infty}$. Furthermore, the research explores the connection between the moments of the amplitudes and the corresponding sum rules.

Researchers have suggested the application of quantum interferometry and information processing in Bose-Einstein condensates. Employing an innovative approach based on nonlinear physics and guided by the principle of minimal wave function variation, a method for generating control operators in quantum systems has been developed without referencing underlying dynamics. This novel technique's fundamental ambiguity is resolved by imposing the operator-valued function's unitarity constraint. The newly formulated method's efficacy is demonstrated through implementations of various linear and nonlinear rotations in systems characterized by unlimited dimensions and interacting bosons. Notably, our technique surpasses traditional control mechanisms by requiring fewer commands to execute the same operation. The differences in functionality between linear and nonlinear controllers have also been examined, revealing distinct behavior during periods of weak interaction. The investigation highlights opportunities for dimension reduction in nonlinear quantum processing and serves as a foundation for exploring novel, highly customizable quantum protocols.

The extended BMS algebra generated by supertranslation and superrotation vector fields at null infinity is predicted to be the symmetry algebra of the quantum gravity S-matrix. However, determining the algebra of quantized extended BMS charges has proven challenging. Recent advancements in celestial holography suggest that the asymptotic charges can be reinterpreted as quantum operators on a Fock space of soft particles, an idea motivated by the CEFT framework. We confirm this notion through applying the CEFT approach to null infinity, effectively recovering the asymptotic charges as operators that create or annihilate multiple soft particles. Furthermore, our work extends the concept of double soft theorems to gravity and N particles, and demonstrates their compatibility with the extended BMS algebra. We also explores the implications of these findings in relation to asymptotic charges in gauge theories with null data and their connection to the asymptotic symmetry algebra of null infinity.

Learning with an ever-growing number of categories poses significant challenges. The task becomes particularly demanding when models need to learn online after seeing each example only once. Current techniques often rely on methods like replay, rehearsal, and memory, low-loss retraining, and online fine-tuning, but there is a lack of comprehensive research in this area. This work fills the gap by presenting a thorough examination of several techniques, including a novel method using support vectors net. The research involves evaluating various approaches on three benchmark datasets. A comprehensive comparison of the techniques is presented, along with a discussion of their strengths and limitations, and future research opportunities are also explored.

In metric geometry and particularly in Riemannian geometry, research involves specific four-dimensional metrics. The primary focus lies on cohomological and characteristic forms associated with these metrics, which have already been explored in complex differential geometry under the name of holomorphic forms. Our investigation demonstrates that in the general case of a non-Riemannian generalized Ricci flat four-metric, the cohomological class of the preferred 2-form is closed. This finding has significant implications in metric geometry, which will be discussed in detail. Additionally, in the context of complex differential geometry, specifically for Kähler manifolds, the study finds that a non-zero holomorphic 2-form, when squared, yields a compatible metric that qualifies as Ricci flat.

In the wake of several recently constructed permutation polynomials over finite fields with square orders, our focus shifts to analyzing permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders through a detailed examination of their coefficients. Utilizing the multivariate method and resultant elimination techniques, we establish novel categories of sparse permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders, with various degrees of completeness, for any $q=p^{k}$ where the prime $p$ exceeds $2$.

Approximately $4$ billion individuals worldwide are affected by intestinal
parasites. The health risks associated with these infections cause a multitude
of issues, such as malnutrition and increased susceptibility to life-threatening
diseases. Notwithstanding its importance, manual classification by specialists is
still the standard approach due to limited knowledge in the field. The process
of manual classification is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and susceptible to
human error. The application of computational methods, particularly image
analysis, offers significant potential in classifying intestinal parasites from
stool samples samples. This study proposes the application of Deep Belief
Networks for intestinal parasites image classification. To our knowledge, this
research represents the initial foray into applying DBN for this classification
task.

This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of zero-sum-free stochastic differential investment and reinsurance models. It incorporates both proportional reinsurance and loss-overlimit reinsurance models. To calculate the Nash equilibrium, a Markov chain approximation approach and a dynamical programming technique are used to solve nonlinear integro-differential Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations. In addition, the research shows the convergence of the approximating sequences to the accurate solution of the value functions, which is supported by several numerical case studies.

This research presents a novel Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) control strategy, integrating a derivative filter, to enhance quadcopter stability in chaotic and unpredictable flight conditions. The mathematical framework is established based on a highly accurate model that effectively accounts for non-linearities, uncertainty, and interdependence. The integration of measurement noise and uncertainty is represented by a linear equation with time-variant coefficients, necessitating real-time solution for control variables. The evaluation of PIDA controller relies on numerous simulations with artificially added noise. The outcomes demonstrate that the proposed controller, paired with an advanced Genetic Filter, successfully navigates through quadcopter models written in MATLAB, accurately addressing positioning errors and maintaining stability even under intense disturbance conditions that mimic real-world unsteady atmospheric conditions.

A comprehensive examination of pion-nucleon interactions at low energy is provided,
with the underlying mechanics of isospin being thoroughly explored.
The isospin decomposition of scattering amplitudes is discussed in detail,
with cross-checks to established experimental findings.
The isospin basis, rather than the coupled-channel nucleon form, is used for the analysis.
The utilization of this isospin basis offers a novel perspective on conventional techniques.
The isospin decomposition also offers insights into Chiral Effective Field Theory and systematic evaluations.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment will upgrade its detector for the LHC's third run with new components, including improved silicon sensors for the tracker.  The novel sensor design will be tested with a specialized module during the LHC's run 2.  The module, referred to as a Pilot Blade, is an advanced version of the regular silicon sensor component and is being used in the experiment's insertion traccker.  The Pilot Blade is an individual blade with a unique design featuring new silicon sensor technology that is being implemented for the LHC's run 2.  The CMS collaboration has successfully reconstructed particles produced in proton-proton collisions that took place at a collision energy of 13 TeV and recorded during the CMS experiment's commissioning phase.  The results of the new-module analysis are presented in this report.  The CMS collaboration has also released a comparison chart illustrating the performance of the new silicon sensor technology.  The new silicon sensor technology is being implemented for the new CMS tracker insertions.  The chart provides a visual representation that the performance of the new silicon sensor technology is within the acceptable limits set by CMS.

We have developed a machine learning-based system to accurately identify the types of Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) host galaxies within the first billion years of the universe's existence. To test its effectiveness, we compared the outcomes of two distinct machine learning models on a subset of approximately 8000 galaxies from the Second Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide Survey Drift Campaign dataset. One model relied on a compact galaxy sample obtained through visual inspections for training, while the other was trained using a subset of galaxies classified through visual inspections as non-AGN or AGN host galaxies. Both models demonstrated strong classification ability, with the first model's performance on unknown data reaching 94% and the second model reaching 85%. Furthermore, we successfully determined the general galaxy type (i.e. elliptical or Lenthermic) with classification rates of approximately 90% for the first model and 79% for the second. We discovered that machine learning can accurately classify AGN host galaxies based on their overall appearance. We investigated the characteristics of AGN host galaxies based on their types by analyzing their color, size, mass, and rate of star formation patterns. We found that Lenthermic galaxies tend to possess the characteristics of irregular, star-forming galaxies, while elliptical galaxies resemble old, starless galaxies. We are working to determine how these types of AGN host galaxies change as the universe gets older.

High-energy and high-momentum fluctuations in the one-body density matrix of a nucleus are a key indicator of short-range correlations between nucleons. Employing the Hartree-Fock method with the Skyrme forces, researchers have mapped the amplitude of this density matrix as a function of energy and momentum, enabling a comprehensive analysis of correlations within the nucleus. Compared to the inert gas krypton, nuclei without a pair of nucleons that undergoes a deformation when their angular momentum is paired exhibit more energy and momentum fluctuations in their one-body density matrix. Furthermore, the fluctuations in this matrix are more pronounced in the nucleons found close to the nucleus's surface than those that reside in the nucleus's center. In contrast, the presence of paired nucleons in deformed nuclei like the inert gas krypton leads to reduced fluctuations in the one-body density matrix. In the future, researchers aim to quantify the amplitude of correlations as a function of energy and momentum using experimental data from experiments involving high-energy electrons and protons that interact with the nucleus.

We are studying complex scaling as an inherent property unique to complex number systems and its implications for deep complex models. By extending the complex domain to its co-domain without restricting to real outcomes, we can develop more effective and flexible models. This concept of complex scaling has significant practical applications in industries such as audio (speech enhancement, speech generation) and computer vision (image enhancement, image creation). To leverage complex scaling, we propose novel loss functions, including a Pearson divergence extension for complex outputs and a mean squared error adaptation for paired complex values. Experimental results show that the proposed methods consistently produce better results, with notable improvements in the case of complex scaling.

The non-linear QCD evolution equations ultimately lead to the saturation of parton densities at large energies, resulting in several notable consequences such as the emergence of geometric scaling effects within specific energy intervals. Several key features associated with geometric scaling have been experimentally validated through various studies on Deep Inelastic ep Scattering. This research also discovered a connection between certain scaling behaviors and the formation of geometric scaling; for example, the dynamics of quark scaling is directly linked to the gluon saturation phenomenon. This phenomenon, governed by the gluon saturation momentum scale, can be used to predict a geometric scaling effect within a particular energy interval. This article explores the concept of saturation and geometric scaling within the context of ep scattering and Heavy Ion Collisions, with a particular focus on their underlying physical mechanisms.

A significant challenge in understanding metal-poor star formation lies in the differences in metal content, or abundance dispersion. Through a comprehensive analysis using detailed chemical compositions of 88 metal-poor stars with ages estimated to be over 10 billion years, we found that the source of abundance dispersion is not solely due to the varying rates of nucleosynthesis based on metal content. Stars with the lowest levels of metal content exhibit a statistically significant, clumpy distribution of abundance dispersion, indicating that variability in nucleosynthesis based on metal content exists across multiple sources. Additionally, we found that the variation in abundance measured for individual elements contributes to the overall dispersion more significantly than the variation in age of the stars.

A novel machine learning approach has been developed that identifies and measures the potential impact of omitted significant predictors on predictive models. The algorithm extends the capabilities of machine learning, enabling not only predictive tasks but also robust inference and sensitivity analysis. An empirical example demonstrates its practicality, showcasing its ability to be applied in data sets containing ordered categorical variables, which are common in education research.

This research introduces SQUID, an open-source tool for developing and training hybrid Quantum-Classical classification algorithms. It utilizes PyTorch for the classical components, allowing for the creation of multiple quantum models that can be optimized with back-propagation. We demonstrate SQUID's capabilities by showcasing its implementation in a standard binary classification task from the widely-used MNIST dataset. Notably, we discuss how the choice of output affects the scalability of quantum models when utilizing gradient-based optimization.

Researchers, Chen and Garay, have examined pointwise slant submanifolds in almost Hermitian manifolds. By extending the concept of slant submanifolds to semi-slant ones, this study delves into their geometry in both Sasakian and cosymplectic manifolds. Key findings indicate a limitation on semi-slant warped products in Sasakian manifolds. On the other hand, non-trivial semi-slant warped products have been discovered in cosymplectic manifolds, and several foundational results have been obtained, including a defining characteristic of such semi-slant warped products.

The PALEOCCENE concept has the potential to develop sensitive and efficient low-energy detectors that can operate at room temperature and are minimally maintained. Such detectors could range in weight from grams to kilograms and are capable of detecting rare events with extraordinary precision. The process involves utilizing the movement of atomic particles around a color center within a crystal structure to convert weak interactions into measurable changes in the center's state. Several color center systems including diamond, alpha-silicon carbide, and strontium iodide serve as the foundation for this idea. Initially, PALEOCCENE systems may utilize high-energy nuclear reactions rather than neutron scattering to create the desired effects. The resulting systems could not only detect low-energy recoil events but also create novel opportunities for basic scientific research including the study of unusual radioactivity and the precise measurement of weak interactions.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. For a dimer oriented perpendicularly, it moves along the gradient, fluctuating between different activity levels. These findings are confirmed by a numerical simulation.

We investigate numerically charge-neutral collective excitations in fractional quantum Hall systems, focusing on two specific examples: a numerical simulation of the $ν=1/3\) system and an anisotropic triangular lattice model. We demonstrate that the characteristic features in the spectral function of the simulated $ν=1/3$ system and the recent experimental findings of Zhang et al. are consistent with the predictions derived from the established sum rules of the $ab$-plane current operator. Furthermore, we show that specific residual contributions violate these sum rules at low energies. We also identify additional collective excitations that might be mistaken for the "magnetoroton" observed in recent experiments, leading to an enhanced resonance peak in the spectral function.

Epidemics on massive contact networks with millions of individuals pose significant challenges for analysis and containment due to their immense scale. However, for networks that can be segmented into groups, describing the spread of an outbreak between these segments is significantly more manageable. Typically, studies have relied on dividing individuals into categories based on characteristics such as age or occupation. In this study, we adopt a more abstract and general approach, focusing on clusters as a means of organizing the network. A geometric representation is then utilized to identify the SIR model's dynamics between these clusters, leading to the development of simplified models for small-scale outbreaks. This simplified framework is particularly useful for computational purposes, enabling the identification of essential parameters with reduced resource demand.

The maximum likelihood estimator used in CMB map-making provides the most efficient way to minimize instrumental noise effects in the final maps. However, this method has the drawback of introducing 'x'-shaped artifacts centered around strong point sources, which can be particularly problematic for deep surveys featuring a high density of sources. We investigate the underlying causes of the artifacts and compare the performance of two alternative point source handling methods integrated into a full end-to-end simulation framework. These methods are combined with a new implementation of the maximum likelihood estimator, which we use to simulate CMB maps in a step-by-step mapping process. Our tests show that by implementing either of these methods, it's possible to eliminate the artifacts present in the maximum likelihood-based maps produced, making them a viable choice for upcoming CMB experiments.

Interpreting teaching instructions with objects and their qualities is complicated by the fact that multiple properties of a single object can conform to the given description. Yet, educators typically use concise language in teaching agents about the world, which poses the challenge of how to effectively communicate complex relationships between objects and qualities. In this research, we address this challenge by creating a set of instructive tasks derived from a situation where a trainer tasks an agent with finding and collecting specific fruits in a room. In this scenario, the key is to differentiate between fruits and other objects in the room. We design these tasks to test the capabilities of two cutting-edge reinforcement learning techniques that focus on achieving set objectives: model-based relabeling and value iteration. We also compare the performance of these models with that of PMTL, a more advanced method of reinforcement learning that is able to interpret natural language instructions. Our findings indicate that PMTL is able to adapt quickly and achieve set objectives with minimal supervision, which goes beyond its ability to learn from general experience. This research extends the current understanding of PMTL by showing that it is able to effectively interpret complex teaching instructions.

Quantum process tomography is crucial for assessing and developing quantum devices.
We introduce an advanced approach called shadow process tomography that provides
a more efficient quantum characterization tool. Shadow process tomography excels
in two key areas: it necessitates less quantum resource usage, specifically less
needs for an initial quantum channel setup, and it necessitates fewer classical
data collections. The new method leverages channel-induced matrix shadow
operators to determine process matrices through least squares and statistical
propagation. We apply this approach on random quantum channels and showcase
its effectiveness by presenting the presented results compared to traditional
quantum process tomography methods.

We aim to derive precise bounds for the Cheeger constant using a range of geometric attributes such as area, perimeter, inradius, circumradius, minimum width and diameter. Our approach involves establishing tight inequalities among these measures specifically for planar convex bodies, along with formulating new conjectures that stem from numerical experiments.

This study investigates the optimization of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) flight paths to maximize the signals received by mobile users on the ground, taking into account time constraints. Specifically, we analyze a communications system consisting of a single UAV carrying a modulated signal, mobile users with varying initial knowledge of the signal, and a pilot phase, which allocates resources to users based on their channel conditions, after which the UAV continues on a predetermined trajectory. To address this problem, we first prove the feasibility of supporting all ground users with a specified signal using a volume of the signal's coverage that can be controlled through the UAV's position. We then develop an algorithm maximizing the combined signal strengths from the UAV, which is geometrically equivalent to moving objects within a polyhedron space. This problem is known to be complex and difficult to solve optimally; instead, we employ a novel algorithm based on the direction $(\lambda_{max}-\lambda_i)$ of the eigenvalues from the UAV's channel matrix, which enables distribution of the pilot phase resources to the user with the weakest signal strength. We demonstrate the efficiency of this algorithm via simulation results showcasing its performance compared to a baseline method.

The low-energy electronic structure of an unbiased bilayer graphene, characterized by quadratic dispersions at two Fermi points when high-order contributions are disregarded, differs qualitatively from that of single-layer graphene. We found that this difference leads to short-range interactions that are marginally relevant. Through the use of the renormalization group to investigate these interactions' effects on the system's properties, it was observed that, at zero temperature, the two quadratic Fermi points would spontaneously divide into four Dirac points, giving rise to a nematic state with lattice symmetry breaking. In this nematic state, the system's six-fold lattice rotation symmetry, along with its layer permutation, decreases to a two-fold one. Moreover, this phenomenon occurs at a non-zero transition temperature, with its critical properties as well as the impact of trigonal warping having been discussed.

Research into nanomaterials based on transition metal nitride clusters has gained significant momentum in the field of materials science and physics. Studying these nanomaterials at the atomic scale is crucial to grasping their unique properties and versatile applications. Our investigation focuses on the structural properties of Sc2TbN@C80 deposited on a hexagonal boron nitride substrate with a nickel (111) layer, employing atomic resolution scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy. Our results show that the structure of Sc2TbN@C80 undergoes a change in conformation as a function of temperature, with evidence suggesting that the Tb atom exhibits magnetic properties with a clear spin resonance at about 0.43 eV, aligning with historical data. Our findings also indicate that the Tb atom's magnetic properties remain intact even when the cluster is in its higher energy structure configuration at 42 K.

The internet of things encompasses a network of interconnected devices, which includes various non-standard gadgets, traditionally unlinked to the internet, at an exponentially growing pace. Data security and user privacy concerns loom large over the IoT landscape, where devices operate on low power. Conventional encryption methods are unsuitable for these devices, necessitating a need for contemporary lightweight algorithms tailored for IoT settings on low power devices such as microcontrollers. This study provides an overview of the IoT's structure, encompassing aspects of hardware, network, application software, security, and user privacy, with a focus on encryption techniques suitable for low power devices like microcontrollers.

The Ramsey sequence serves as a prime illustration of quantum phase measurement for a spin 1/2 system, widely employed across various scientific disciplines. To optimize measurement outcomes under constraints, a novel adaptive experimental design method is developed and implemented for the Ramsey sequence. This approach, grounded in sequential Bayesian statistics, continuously monitors the posterior distribution of the parameter in question and selects the most effective subsequent measurement time parameter. To demonstrate the well-functioning design method, a Bayesian optimization technique is implemented in a quantum memory-based system, enabling the inherent noise to be identified and assessed. Notably, the results show that this adaptive design technique can achieve 90 percent of the accuracy level attained by the optimal (ideal) experimental setup, despite the inherent noise, thereby ensuring high accuracy in phase measurements. This research highlights the significance of the adaptive experimental design method in achieving optimal results in various scientific investigations.

Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using distinct, straightforward mathematical programs that capture distinct aspects of a network's structure. At one end, the maximum flow program defines a node's importance on a global scale, related to its influence across the entire network, while the minimum cut program represents its importance on a local scale, related to its importance for nearby nodes. This article introduces a new centrality metric, Gromov centrality, which, like others, defines importance through the minimum cut program, but focuses on a multi-scale approach by incorporating variations that capture the node's importance within smaller subsets of the network. It does this using a triangle inequality excess measure that can be interpreted as a new class of network centrality metrics. This approach is tested and evaluated by comparing it with other established centrality metrics, including closeness and betweenness centrality, using a range of network examples. At the same time, a theoretical link is made between a new variation of the Gromov centrality and a maximum flow programme that defines a node's importance on an even larger scale, showing how the Gromov centrality can capture information at different network scales.

The work presents the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation, a theoretical framework that belongs to the class of two-metric theories of gravitation. It postulates the existence of both gravitational force fields, fulfilling Einstein's general relativity, as well as secondary force fields. These secondary fields are detectable but exhibit significantly weaker effects. The theory's mathematical implementation involves an advanced method of solving the system of nonlinear equations that define the metric tensors. The derivations show that the effects exhibited by the secondary fields are characterized by the fourth power of the distance from the source of gravitation. Moreover, the theory predicts that these secondary fields are generated by mass concentrations exhibiting uniform radial symmetry. The theoretical framework can be accurately reduced to Newton's law of gravitation, the law of a sphere, and the Einstein equations. The theoretical model appears to be compatible with the Mossbauer rotation moody effect, as well as the Perihelion shift in the orbit of a planet.

Sets of matrix pencils sharing the same Kronecker canonical form are classified under strict equivalence into infinite groups called bundles. Introduced in 1992, this concept was initially motivated by seeking critical points on a specific parameter space in control theory. Each matrix pencil within a bundle can be seen as a point in two different projections of the same subset in a parameter space. The study of these bundles in the realm of matrix pencils was extensive, with emerging applications in systems theory, but the concept remains unexplored for matrix boxes, a higher-dimensional analogue of matrix pencils. This work delves into the theory of bundles for matrix boxes under strict equivalence. We identify two distinct types of bundles for matrix boxes: those that arise from box Kronecker canonical form and others with reduced size. The infinite group of matrix boxes constituting each bundle can be defined through specific local invariants. The concept of matrix box bundles offers various practical applications, aligning with the objectives set forth in the original matrix pencil bundle introduction. Each infinite group of matrix boxes, comprising matrix pencils that share the same Kronecker canonical form, corresponds to a subset in parameter spaces of increasing dimensions. The size of these subsets is finite, with matrix boxes forming critical points on these spaces. The study of matrix box bundles, with its infinite groups defined by two distinct local invariants, allows for a generalization of the matrix pencil bundle concept.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By generalizing the T-duality transformation for compact Lie groups to noncompact settings, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between the topological spaces of twistor form and those of topological origin. This correspondence is realized through the representation of the twistor form $C^*$-algebra as a subalgebra within a cross product algebra constructed from the topological model, thereby demonstrating T-duality from the perspective of $C^*$-algebras.

Cohen-Addad, Filtser, Klein, and Le established that any metric of diameter $D$ and treewidth $\tau$ can be embedded into a tree of diameter $O(D\log\tau)$ and treewidth $O(\log\tau)$.  Building on this, we introduce a new method for embedding metrics, which yields embeddings with treewidth $O(\log n)$ for metrics on $n$ points, with only a single logarithmic dependence on the diameter.  This method is demonstrated on minor-free metrics and, when combined with a known result, also holds for planar metrics.  Our technique leverages a novel algorithm, known as the Black-Box Embedding Algorithm, which improves upon previous embedding methods.  As the Black-Box Algorithm relies on an existing embedding algorithm, any advancement in embedding technique contributes to the development of a better black-box embedding.  Furthermore, the Black-Box Algorithm enables a simplified implementation of many existing embedding algorithms, which results in a more compact and transparent proof.  As a direct application, we present a new and more efficient proof for Cohen-Addad et al.'s algorithm.  Additionally, the Black-Box Algorithm has potential applications in solving problems efficiently, such as approximating the cost of a minimum spanning tree, which was a key element in the original Cohen-Addad et al. method.

For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing long-term behavior of linearly stable cycles is established in a probabilistic framework. This research then extends to periodic parabolic equations and reveals new findings regarding the ubiquity of periodic solution convergence. Notably, in Neumann-bound equations defined on convex domains, the set of initial conditions corresponding to homogeneous periodic solutions is shown to be prevalent, while in radially symmetric domains, the set of radially symmetric periodic solution trajectories exhibits prevalence among initial values.

The potential of using variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) to solve eigenvalue problems, utilizing quantum computers, is crucial to the utilization of quantum computers. One current limitation of VQE is that it employs the state of the quantum bit (qubit) in its ground state, therefore necessitating an additional step to calculate excitation energies. Herein, we propose the adaptation of VQE, utilizing the excitation of the quantum bit, specifically the $x$- and $y$-polarized excitation, referred to as $x$-XAN and $y$-YAN. We demonstrate that $x$-XAN and $y$-YAN outperform the conventional VQE method in terms of accuracy across a range of studies involving single-coordinated molecules, without necessitating reinitialization of the quantum bit into its ground state. We also demonstrate that $x$-XAN and $y$-YAN utilize fewer quantum gates compared to VQE. We are able to execute $y$-YAN on IBM's 5T QROM qubit under the IBM Q experience. We are able to compare the convergence speed of $x$-XAN, $y$-YAN, and VQE on IBM Q experience for a quantum simulation of the 4-coordinated hydrogen molecule. A crucial choice in deep generative models is the encoder, which selects initial characteristics from input data. We contend that a standard maximum likelihood encoder is not the optimal choice, due to its potential for producing distorted representations that compromise the model's performance. In this study, we explore an alternative approach, where the encoder is replaced by a "deep generative decoder," which uses a Bayesian estimate of the latent variables based on the model's prior and likelihood distributions. We examine the properties of this decoder and its implications for a specific type of model, the Gaussian latent variable model. We also investigate practical methods for approximating the soft encoder, a technique which can be applied to a broader range of models. Experimental findings demonstrate that the proposed approach is effective in reducing the encoder's impact on a deep generative model, resulting in improved latent variable quality. This discovery has significant potential to enhance latent variable research and modeling in the field of deep generative models.

The discovery of a common-spectrum component in gravitational waves by NANOGrav has led to two possible explanations: either there is an astrophysical source that has yet to be identified, or these waves could be the result of primordial waves generated during the inflationary period. If the primordial waves are true and are observed at a frequency of around 10-100 nHz, they would need to have gone through amplification due to the dynamics of the early universe. Two possible scenarios include either the perturbations being part of the dark energy sector or having a steeper spectrum. A stiff gravitational wave background could provide evidence for an inflationary model. Researchers have calculated how the energy density of these waves would change over time and have applied these calculations to several models including one where the steeper spectrum meets the criteria for the Planck data and the cosmological observations from BAO, CMB and the observations of the Lyman-alpha forest. A cold, molecular coma from comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) was detected using ALMA Atacama Compact Array on April 12, 2017, and molecular emissions including CN, C2H2, and HCN, as well as sulfur compounds, were found. The comet's gas production was observed at high resolution during its 2017 apparition, providing insights into the unique CN molecule. The model fit molecular emissions with a total gas production rate of 1.7 x 10^28 molecules per second. The models also indicated that gas production was centered at 2,500 kilometers from the nucleus' center, suggesting that CN, C2H2, and HCN originated from a particular region of the nucleus' surface, while sulfur compounds likely originated from a different area.
