Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, resulting in a significant decline in urban diversity. To study the impact of these restrictions, researchers analyzed two years of data (2019-2021) from GPS devices used by ride-hailing drivers in multiple cities, focusing on changes in diversity during the pandemic in Los Angeles, New York City, and Seattle. Their findings indicated a substantial (6-fold) decrease in diversity, which differed significantly from the minor fluctuations observed prior to the pandemic. Moreover, a closer examination revealed that increased COVID-19 cases, stricter movement limitations, and tighter quarantine measures led to further reductions in diversity, underscoring the complex interplay of factors contributing to its decline.

This research evaluates the effectiveness of various nonlinear field-decomposition approaches in resolving two-phase fluid movement within complex media. Five techniques - Balancing Domain Decomposition Method, Advanced Balancing Domain Decomposition Method, Full Domain Decomposition Method, Successive Over-Relaxation, and Newton Over-Relaxation - were tested against highly disparate scenarios. The findings indicate that the most versatile method is the Balancing Domain Decomposition Method, as it excels in both fast and slow convergence situations. Further analysis is presented in a series of presentations in Lecture 1 and detailed findings in Report 2023-02.

The property of chirality exists ubiquitously in nature, featuring predominantly in molecules, biomolecules, and antennas. Chiral entities exhibit different physical characteristics for left- and right-handed versions. This study explores a novel type of optical cavity with a single-handed property, supported by two mirrors, one reflective and the other transparent to light. Geometrical asymmetry in the structure gives rise to the phenomenon. The optical properties of the cavity can be fully defined by two key parameters - the orientation angle and polarization of light. Experimental results demonstrate the prevalence of uniform mode polarization within the cavity, accompanied by the disappearance of anti-dominant mode polarization. The observed unidirectional emission from the chiral cavity is attributed to the reflection of light by the mirror. Additionally, research findings show the possibility of adjusting the orientation angle of emitted light beams by modifying the position of a placed aperture. The study of the chiral cavity may contribute to a deeper understanding of chirality in nature and facilitate the creation of chirality-based optical devices and systems.

This paper examines the connection between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity on anti de-Sitter spaces and a semi-classical limit of two-dimensional string theory, with c less than 1. We observe that the world-sheet theory of this string theory, comprising a space and time dependent Liouville and zero-mode CFT couple, shares traits with the Seiberg bound of the c extremal Liouville theory. We then deduce that the pair of Liouville CFTs with zero-modes, coupled with JT gravity on an extremal BTZ black hole, exhibits modular invariance symmetry. We also investigate the action of this Liouville CFT pair and find it mirroring the extremal c Liouville theory's boundary action. We then discuss possible implications on the change in the Lyapunov exponent, in the two models.

A spacetime distortion, or warp bubble, generated by the Alcubierre metric can enable massive objects to achieve global speeds faster than light. This study focuses on a specific warp drive model, where a perfect fluid drives the spacetime, without a matter component within the bubble. We've discovered and developed two novel solutions for the warp core, each incorporating the cosmological constant and differing initial conditions. These solutions not only provide complete spatial locations but also the full temporal evolution of the warp core geometry, allowing for the analysis of metric features such as singularities, horizons, and conformal relationships. We've also explored how the fundamental properties of the warp drive remain unaltered by the inclusion of the cosmological constant, particularly in terms of exponential slip functions and conformal relationships.

As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require growing upkeep, cities are faced with the challenge of coordinating and understanding maintenance, asset management, and planning for the underground infrastructure they house. Cities have expressed a need for integrated and standardized data management platforms that can consolidate diverse infrastructure data from various sources, facilitating the creation of a comprehensive digital twin of their underground infrastructure. To address this need, the CITYSEED project has developed the GUIDES framework, a data engineering solution for consolidating and standardizing non-conformal underground infrastructure data from diverse sources. The GUIDES framework consists of a set of tools for processing, a data catalog for metadata management, and a data platform for integrated infrastructure data. By establishing a core dataset and breaking down non-conformal data into four distinct components, the GUIDES framework enables seamless data integration. The GUIDES platform accommodates geospatial data from diverse sources through the use of a semistructured data model and APIs for data access. The GUIDES framework encompasses both the data platform and the processing tools, as well as data governance principles and policies, making it a comprehensive data engineering solution. The GUIDES framework was demonstrated through the analysis of sewer network data, which included the extraction of geospatial features from diverse datasets. The analysis of GUIDES platform demonstrated a high degree of consistency among the extracted geospatial features from various datasets. The GUIDES framework was evaluated through a comprehensive assessment of its data processing capabilities, the effectiveness of its data management policies,

To analyze the center-of-mass motion of hundreds of $^{24}$Mg$^+$ ions, arranged in a two-dimensional crystal, we utilized the interaction between the ions' spin and the crystal's collective oscillations. By increasing the ion-internal-state trapping potential while maintaining the crystal's stability, we were able to measure the average temperature of the ions' translational degrees of freedom. Our approach also enabled us to acquire detailed information about the initial motional state distributions with minimal influence on the crystal's structure. We were able to distinguish between different modes of heat dissipation and identify the primary source of excess noise during the crystal's formation, thereby providing a basis for evaluating the reliability of other techniques for analyzing this process.

TERS is a promising technique for local chemical analysis, offering resolution down to 1 nanometer. Yet, accurately interpreting TERS spectra remains challenging due to the complex interaction between the electron and the vibrational modes of the sample molecules and the electromagnetic tip. The electron exchange between the sample and the tip also raises further uncertainties. In an effort to address these complexities, researchers have developed a novel quantum model simulating the electron and electromagnetic interactions. The model successfully replicates the TERS spectra of dichlorobenzene, a crucial test for local analysis methods. The simulation results suggest that a lack of full quantum coherence in the light emitted by the electromagnetic tip is key to explaining the distortions in TERS spectra. The study's findings provide valuable insights for interpreting and enhancing TERS spectra. The model's code is accessible through GitHub under the username chenyu1999.

We used the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope to study the emission of nearby spiral and irregular galaxies in the K-band through a 3-minute observation. The sample consisted of 24 galaxies including M31, M33, and other nearby galaxies. We focused on detecting radiation similar to the Cosmic Infrared Background and the Anomalous Microwave Emission produced by thermal dust particles over large distances. To enhance our sensitivity, we analyzed the data multiple times using different bandwidths, integration times, and signal weights. However, no emission exceeding the noise level in the SKA1 low band was detected. We then used the data to establish upper limits on the thermal dust power law slope and amplitude for each galaxy, providing new constraints for galaxy radiation. The limits we found are consistent with the power laws for irregular and spiral galaxies. The data also show that the thermal dust power law amplitude for the two large spiral galaxies we studied is less than 0.02, indicating very low levels of Anomalous Microwave Emission.

Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated nature belies a significant ferroelectric phase transition accompanied by an exceptionally large entropy variation and both electrocaloric and barocaloric properties. For decades, researchers have disputed the underlying cause of the significant entropy change, but this issue is now resolved using a comprehensive approach that incorporates density functional theory-based phonon calculations, inelastic neutron scattering, and additional neutron scattering experiments. In contrast to the previously assumed, albeit widely adopted model of entropy involving disorder across the high-symmetry phase's mirror plane, it is now clear that this simplistic model is invalid. Instead, it is discovered that significant lattice vibrations in ammonium sulfate's high-symmetry phase involve considerable ammonia group motion within this unit cell. Consequently, it is now possible to explain the large entropy change associated with the solid's phase transition. Furthermore, due to the complex ammonia group motion involved, it is demonstrated that the system exhibits complex vibrational characteristics, encompassing single, double, and quasi-localized modes. This understanding also highlights the importance of ammonia groups in driving solid-state ferroelectricity.

In probabilistic learning, organisms often switch from optimal strategies due to varying levels of reward expectations, which diverge from the actual outcomes. Prior studies in humans and animals have found suboptimal decision-making tends to appear in distinct midbrain activity, suggesting an objective neural underlying process. This study combines electroencephalography and behavioral tasks to investigate how midbrain activity relates to the phenomenon of suboptimal strategies. We found that participants who demonstrated suboptimal strategies showed more pronounced midbrain activity in response to outcomes that diverged from expectations. Furthermore, midbrain activity in response to positive outcomes that exceeded expectations significantly predicted the occurrence of suboptimal strategies. Notably, individual differences in this midbrain activity were stable across time and correlated with midbrain activity in response to error in a different learning paradigm, indicating a common underlying trait. In contrast, the correlation between midbrain activity in error tasks and the occurrence of suboptimal strategies was only significant in cases where participants reported low levels of uncertainty. These findings imply that midbrain encoding of unanticipated positive outcomes shares a common underlying nature with the occurrence of suboptimal strategies and may be a manifestation of a complex and adaptable behavioral pattern.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 systems based on a dodecahedron's geometry, to study quantum mechanics' nonlocality and contextuality. An alternative setup using 120 states is examined in this work. Despite the vast system, the configurations' possible measurements and resulting outcomes can be calculated directly from the root system due to their limited number, at least in the simplified model. An examination of 16 special roots indicates that many of the resulting configurations are strong and nonlocal. In the simplified model, at least 5 new types of non-Cauchy nonlocality were identified, along with several non-Cauchy contextuality instances. The configurations' complexity also permits the analysis of their nonlocality and contextuality averages, which were found to have clear maxima. The study of the simplified model may facilitate a more in-depth analysis of the original Witting configuration's geometry, ultimately advancing our understanding of quantum mechanics' fundamental principles.

The continuous Fréchet distance c-approximate near neighbor problem involves precomputing a data structure that efficiently finds closest polygonal curves within a certain radius from query curves, considering an approximation factor for potential inaccuracies. This study primarily investigates this problem using time series curves, providing a comprehensive analysis for one-dimensional curves. By improving existing results, the research offers multiple tradeoffs between approximation quality, preprocessing efficiency, and query speed. Key outcomes include achieving the same performance as the previously best result for an improved approximation factor while also reaching the previously best result with reduced query complexity. Additionally, softer approximation methods using the Hausdorff distance were also explored, providing a comprehensive overview of findings in this direction.

To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee a correct probability distribution cannot be scaled. To address these concerns, we propose a new scheme that combines the principles of iterative Bayesian unfolding to combat systematic errors. Our approach is tested on simulations of a quantum simulator running the Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm, using both realistic error rates and perfect targeting probabilities. In comparison to existing schemes, our method is able to handle a larger number of qubits without producing negative probabilities. Furthermore, its validity can be reinforced using established methods, but it falls short of current state-of-the-art schemes in terms of efficiency. Nonetheless, we believe that the success of this approach paves the way for a range of novel methods that can tackle the complex problem of mitigating systematic errors on quantum computers.

When humans operate robot arms, it is frequently necessary for the robot to infer the task the human is attempting to accomplish. Current research on co-manipulation tasks has demonstrated that humans adapt their movements in response to the expected task. However, the current methods of inferring the desired task are limited to the particular actions the robot is equipped to recognize. To resolve this problem, our study examined whether the internal models of the human operator for executing tasks with varying conventions (such as inserting or picking) can be discerned through an initial period of unguided interaction. Using an evolutionary algorithm, the robot is capable of adapting its movement conventions to minimize delays in task execution. The results of interactions between a humanoid robot and a group of humans revealed that the robot's conventions were able to converge towards the conventions utilized by the human operator, resulting in significant reductions in task inference errors and computation time. The convergence of conventional models was found to outperform other methods of task inference in the field.

For mobile robots to navigate unfamiliar areas, they require a navigation system that automatically constructs and updates a map based on a single integration of on-board sensors, including an inertial unit, camera, and 2D laser scanner. The proposed solution employs a self-organizing topological map to process sensor data and creates a multi-level map, where local areas are connected based on spatial and feature data. To enhance map building, a novel method uses a self-organizing feature learning network to extract meaningful features from sensor data, reducing data complexity and facilitating detection of landmarks. The integrated system was thoroughly tested in a real-world setting utilizing a single platform, demonstrating its capability to navigate and locate itself within a complex environment. According to the evaluation results, the system effectively localizes its surroundings and detected landmarks with minimal errors in an unfamiliar environment.

Research into two-dimensional arrays with favorable two-dimensional correlation properties has gained significant interest due to the rapid advancements in modern wireless communication technologies. Various applications of two-dimensional arrays can be found in areas such as ultra-wide band, 2-D synchronization, and phase noise cancellation. A novel method for creating two-dimensional arrays with favorable two-dimensional correlation properties based on multivariable functions is presented. First, an inter-group complementary code set is constructed using multivariable functions, which satisfies correlation requirements among group symbols. Utilizing the inter-group complementary code set, two-dimensional arrays with favorable two-dimensional correlation properties are developed. These two-dimensional arrays possess zero cross-correlation values in all directions, while their auto-correlation values are unit values.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both medical and industrial applications for creating detailed images of internal structures within various types of objects. Since most materials absorb X-rays at different rates according to their energy, using multiple energy levels can greatly improve the reconstruction of image details and material properties. This paper introduces an innovative variational image reconstruction technique that addresses a range of challenges, including non-ideal sensor performance, varying X-ray energy, and a wide spectrum of noise types. By transforming raw projection data into more meaningful forms, our method effectively minimizes the effects of noise caused by photon counting system flaws. Additionally, our proposed model includes an advanced material decomposition system. Based on the alternating minimization of various image quality metrics, our method is able to optimize image parameters. One key advantage of our approach is its ability to use non-smooth functions to model complex image characteristics. By using Newton-like schemes to solve related optimization problems, our method is able to efficiently solve the convex and non-convex optimization problems that arise. This proposed model is validated through numerical experiments involving both simulated data and actual industrial computed tomography scans.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a new light propagation mechanism, driven by nonlocal electron dynamics, becomes significant at gaps smaller than the electron mean free path. In this regime, the quantum hydrodynamics model provides a more accurate description of light propagation. Conversely, at larger gaps, the light propagation pattern can be accurately predicted using a classical local model based on Maxwell's equations. The influence of the electron spillover on light propagation is relatively minimal in both scenarios.

In this research, we investigate the importance of user input quality in Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER) and develop a simple, efficient approach to enhance term relevance through a pre-training objective called Contextualized Term Relevance Feedback. We employ this innovative method to improve three state-of-the-art CNER systems and observe significant performance boosts in terms of of precision, recall, and F1. Notably, our solutions achieve top-ranked results in the 2021 CoNLL Shared Task on English and Italian, ranking 1st out of 27 in Italian and 2nd out of 28 in English.

Time-based data refers to information measured against the backdrop of time, giving it a distinct structural context that forms the foundation of its constituent parts. When dealing with four or more variables, we classify this data as multivariate, characterized by the interplay between individual component signals and their collective interactions. In contrast, longitudinal data focuses on the progression of a single variable over time, often including additional contextual information about the observed unit. While both types of data can be difficult to comprehend due to the sheer volume of generated data, visualizations aim to simplify the process by leveraging human visual processing capabilities. Nevertheless, the inherent complexity still presents significant challenges to interactive exploration. This article seeks to identify the commonalities and shared obstacles between multivariate time series and longitudinal data, with a particular focus on enabling interactive exploration. We find that both types of data benefit from the visualization of trends, especially through the incorporation of small multiples. Additionally, supervised machine learning models can unlock hidden knowledge by pinpointing correlations and patterns. While these approaches demonstrate a notable history of application, they still rely heavily on human analysis. As the quantity of available data continues to explode, we require more sophisticated methods for annotating and refining our understanding of this data, ideally through the application of unsupervised methods. Finally, we examine how both types of data can be leveraged to gain a more holistic understanding of the underlying system, particularly in cases where the observed units exhibit a high degree of similarity.

The promising potential of extracting valuable insights from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has emerged as a crucial area of study, as machine learning models can assist healthcare professionals in decision-making to enhance overall patient care. Advances in recent years have seen the development of sequential or graph-based machine learning models aiming to tackle the complexities of EHR data. Despite these efforts, most proposed models have treated diverse EHR components as homogeneous elements within a graph structure, overlooking the inherent connections and relationships between various components. This study introduces a novel graph neural network called the Heterogeneous Similarity Graph Neural Network (HSGNN) that treats and models the diverse EHR components as nodes of an asymptotically equivalent graph, preserving their inherent relationships. For improved efficiency, the proposed model leverages a simplified node aggregation approach by using Highway gates, as well as a customized attention mechanism that allows a deeper understanding of EHR properties. The proposed model was evaluated on class-imbalanced datasets extracted from EHRs, which showed superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art graph-based models.

Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform particle sizes and solvent effects, we model the behavior of the electric double layer at the boundary of a charged flexible material. From a free energy model, we calculate the electrostatic potential and number of water and ions within the boundary using coupled differential equations, including the Poisson equation. We discover that solvent effects profoundly impact the electrostatic potential, ion counts, and permittivity of the electrolyte near the boundary of the charged flexible material. Furthermore, we find that taking solvent effects into account intensifies the Donnan potential and demonstrates that within the boundary of fixed charge, ion counts decrease slightly. Additionally, we find that high concentrations of ions and water within the boundary of the charged flexible material decrease the permittivity of the electrolyte near the boundary. Lastly, we find that solvent effects profoundly impact the thickness of the electric double layer at the boundary of the charged flexible material.

Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a highly recommended goal for many researchers. To this end, we annotated a unique dataset, PURE, and derived a new one combining requirements and non-requirements. We refined a BERT model with this dataset and compared its outcomes with well-established models like fastText and ELMo. To challenge the model with more complex text, we compared PURE's performance with experiments conducted on less formal texts like GitHub issues and bug reports.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in multi-user networks with a single central relay that can simultaneously transmit and receive data, including a direct link between the source and destination. A partial combination of packets at the relay minimizes delays, and thus the study focuses on optimizing energy consumption through simultaneous scheduling and power allocation at the relay. Due to the high computational complexity of traditional energy efficiency optimization problems, the research proposes a simplified linear approximation. By reducing the complexity, the problem is reframeed as a convex optimization problem that can be solved efficiently. A comparative study of different scheduling and power allocation schemes is conducted to optimize energy efficiency. Results show that with the optimal linear approximation, a lower computational complexity is achieved while maintaining a close approximation to the original energy efficiency.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to describe the electronic properties of magnetic impurities on a Nb(110) surface in a superconducting state. This model accounts for complex interactions between the impurity and underlying metal surface, incorporating relativistic effects, exchange interactions, and pairing in the metal. It has been established that the interaction between the magnetic impurity and the superconducting electron density is the primary contributing factor to the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states observed at ultra-low temperatures. This was demonstrated through systematic calculations of YSR states formed by a single magnetic Mn atom, which revealed a significant magnetic environment, for a small concentration of Mn atoms. However, in the case of two Mn atoms located on the Nb(110) surface, the theoretical model predicts a reduced magnetic environment, as compared to the single Mn atom scenario. Additionally, the electron spin of the two Mn atoms was found to align in the same direction when they are located in the middle of a dimer structure. This theoretical framework has been successfully validated against experimental data, including the observed splitting of the YSR states formed by a dimer and the emergence of a new YSR state within the superconducting energy gap in the case of a single Mn atom.

Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) can efficiently register and accurately bound point cloud errors for scenes without moving objects.  However, traditional methods struggle in scenes where there are changes in view.  To improve point cloud registration for dynamic scenes, deep learning-based approaches have shown potential.  Despite their accuracy, deep learning-based solutions often provide little insight, which is a concern for safety in applications.  To address this, our paper presents a method to reduce bias in point cloud registration for dynamic scenes.  Leveraging the local geometric structure of interest points, this method involves an image domain filter to improve point cloud registration accuracy.  The proposed DNN filter operates by comparing transformed 3D point maps to construct a histogram of corresponding cell densities, which serves as a template for accurate point cloud registration.  The proposed model, evaluated using a self-driving car dataset, demonstrates significant improvement in point cloud registration accuracy for scenes with changes in view.  The integration of our DNN filter into existing frameworks further enhances system-level performance, accuracy, and reliability.  The proposed system exhibits improved performance with increased resolution while maintaining real-time processing capabilities.  The proposed system also exhibits lower processing complexity with diminished resolution while maintaining equivalent performance.

Satellite images are widely employed across multiple sectors, encompassing 
agriculture, navigation, and urban planning, often resulting in immense 
databases requiring extensive computational power for processing. Deep 
learning methods have recently gained traction for analyzing satellite images. 
Although incredibly efficient, they have inherent limitations, necessitating 
specialized computing infrastructure and large volumes of annotated data.

We suggest a simplified model for describing changes in electronic configuration around a specific energy level in a particular atom under an increased amount of photons relative to the number that can interact with the atom per unit of time. This model can serve as an alternative to more complex theories like the Manousaki model, providing a straightforward statistical approach that's grounded in the core principles of quantum mechanics. To evaluate its validity, we compared our proposed model with the Manousaki model for near-edge absorption spectra and conducted a statistical analysis to show that they are essentially the same. We tested the models against new high-fluence experimental data collected by Donselaer et al. and found that they provide a good fit. Additionally, we applied these models to analyze data from a particular molybdenum-based catalyst, discovering that there are slight differences in how these materials absorb and scatter radiation compared to pure molybdenum.

The application of a Deep Neural Network in Modulation Classification (MC) offers superior performance compared to traditional methods even in scenarios with limited data. However, this approach's vulnerability to adversarial attacks poses significant risks to Deep Neural Network-based MC. An adversarial attack can be carried out by generating a malicious waveform with the purpose of deceiving the Deep Neural Network and causing it to misclassify the modulation type. An adversary may create this waveform by adjusting its amplitude or phase, which may lead to the financial burden of the transmission carrier due to the modified waveform. In response to this issue, a novel method has been developed called Mixture GAN, which creates a diverse set of common adversarial examples for MC. The generated adversarial examples in MC are waveforms that, when classified by the Deep Neural Network, result in a specific type of modulation. The same waveforms, when classified by an alternative method, would produce a different modulation type or type(s) other than the expected one. The goal of the Mixture GAN is to amplify the diversity of adversarial examples to improve the resilience of the Deep Neural Network against adversarial attacks. Additionally, the conventional approach to detecting adversarial attacks involves examining the anomaly of a specific feature. In this work, a novel method has been proposed to identify adversarial attacks by examining the anomaly of the B-spline coefficients in the wavelet transform domain.

Segmentation of multiple sclerosis lesions is a crucial process that allows researchers to study the progression of the disease, its impact on central nervous system tissue, and potential treatment effects. Establishing a universal dataset of annotated clinical images to train AI models poses a significant challenge due to varying imaging techniques, scales, and standards among hospitals. In response, we developed a novel approach to segment spinal cord lesions in MR images, where we initially trained a model on a primary set of datasets with incremental learning. The model was then fine-tuned using interactive segmentation techniques, and we compared its effectiveness with traditional supervised learning methods that rely on extensive, high-quality, and large-scale datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach segments lesions in test images at a 82% performance level, surpassing the 78% achieved by the supervised learning method.

A novel type of metric comparison analogous to Alexandrov comparison is established, 
and its relationship with optimal transport between measures on manifolds and submanifolds 
is explored, along with the definition of optimal maps in this context.

In the past twenty years, research on forward-in-time iterative learning schemes for modeling complex systems using partial differential equations has yielded significant breakthroughs, largely driven by the need for accurate models in areas such as nuclear engineering and fluid dynamics. Traditional learning schemes assume that model-based simulations are merely offset by random noise. However, inherent limitations in model representations due to complexity constraints cause actual simulations to diverge from their predicted counterparts, characterized as model errors. Distinguishing between these noises and error allows for the effective correction of model flaws, but quantifying the error remains an ongoing challenge. Machine learning has emerged as an influential force in science and engineering, enabling the identification and classification of intricate patterns. Inspired by its success, we propose a systematic approach based on deep learning to identify and map complex model errors over time. By incorporating temporal features and error maps into initial model-based simulations, our proposed framework aims to enhance predictive accuracy. This method holds promise for a range of complex systems, including turbulent flows and solar atmospheric conditions.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific star-related signals resulting from gravitational lensing. A simulation tool called PopSyCLE allows users to study the effects of gravitational lensing and magnification caused by point masses such as black holes. This study aims to assess the tool's suitability for simulating primordial black holes that may be made up of different materials and to establish a detection threshold for these black holes based on the strength of the lensing effect.

The behavior of hard wedge-shaped molecules, formed by combining two spheres with a fixed distance, was studied to determine their equilibrium state. By adjusting the size of the smaller sphere, two distinct phases, involving either a straight or bent configuration, were introduced and analyzed. These phases were found to exhibit uniaxial and isotropic properties when the smaller sphere was small in comparison to the larger sphere. These phases were also discovered to exhibit unique nematic and isotropic properties when the smaller sphere was small enough to allow for weak interactions and allow clustering to occur. These phases were found to remain metastable for a wide range of the smaller sphere's size. These phases were discovered to exhibit unique pressure and temperature effects that could separate the two distinct phases, which are found to occur at low pressures and temperatures. These phases were found to exhibit unique entropy and free energy effects that can explain the two distinct phases, which can be represented on a hexagonal crystal structure. These phases were found to exhibit unique vibrational effects that can explain the two distinct phases, which can be represented on a hexagonal crystal structure. These phases were found to exhibit unique molecular dynamics effects. Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
using a limited number of extra tokens to modify the input sequence for adaptation,
instead of utilizing task-specific prompts. By doing so, PASTA can reduce the number
of parameters updated further, leveraging the sequence encoder's ability to process
information in a manner independent of token boundaries. We evaluate PASTA on the
Natural Language Processing Transfer Testing Dataset suite and Findings of PASTA experiments,
where it surpasses previous parameter-efficient tuning approaches by a significant
margin, with a notable improvement of 1.0 EL improvement on NLP-TTS data with only
8 extra tokens.

This paper investigates a complex problem where we need to assess the impact of adding items to a collection. The inherent nature of this problem prevents us from making absolute preferences between options, as adding one item may benefit another. To address this issue, we explored two different approaches: contextual preferences and non-contextual preferences. The former evaluates the impact of each item separately, while the latter considers all items simultaneously. Despite their respective benefits, they have their limitations - the former might not be able to identify when two items have a negative interaction, while the latter can be overly cautious due to the risk of context missing. To address this, we utilized non-contextual preferences with a cut-off score to strike a balance. The combination of these preferences was tested with a real-world dataset and showed a significant improvement in ranking compared to other models.

Our application of the lattice cluster theory for polymer fluids has established that the configurational entropy, enthalpy, and internal energy are interconnected thermodynamic properties as supported by recent neutron scattering and serrano-symmetric dynamics research. The data suggests a thermodynamic model where the total entropy consists of configurational and internal entropies, related in a thermally stable order and also influenced by internal entropy through a debility constraint. The thermodynamic model explains the thermodynamic equilibrium between energetic and non-energetic degrees of freedom and also predicts dynamic behavior controlled by internal entropy. The total entropy also dictates dynamic volatility. The total entropy's changes also predict dynamic connections to heat capacity and speed distributions. The thermodynamic model provides a unified explanation for complex liquid dynamics and information from total, configurational, or internal entropies. The total entropy's characteristics predict dynamic and thermodynamic behavior indicating a unifying role for entropy in glass-forming systems.

Transformer-based language models have been shown to struggle with logical reasoning, especially when it involves negation. Unlike previous studies that relied on psycholinguistic tools, our research delves into types of negation from developmental psychology. We investigate this knowledge gap using a minimal transformation-based approach and uncover distinct behavior patterns from different language models. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that larger language models, including the renowned GPT-3, often Polarisate the meaning of negative statements, instead of Inversing them.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks.

This passage provides an in-depth calculation of the Kontsevich weights for connection and curvature graphs within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on manifolds with a linear symplectic structure. Furthermore, the discussion is expanded to cover deformation weights for tensor fields, with a notable concentration on 1-forms and vector fields.

This research involves determining the large N limit of $O(N)$ models with non-polynomial potential functions in odd dimensional spaces, leading to a new class of interacting conformal field theories. Specifically, this results in CFTs for dimensions 3+4n where n is a positive integer. Calculations of thermal entropy are also carried out for these same dimensions and time periods. It was discovered that in 2+1 dimensions, the ratio of strong-to-weak thermal entropy is 4/5, confirming prior predictions. In higher dimensions, this ratio was found to be constant, specifically 1/n. This suggests a new class of CFTs in odd dimensions that might be used to explain the equivalence between thermal and entanglement entropies.

Cai, Song and Kou made a significant contribution in 2015 by developing a universal approach for pricing Asian options based on one-dimensional Markov processes. This note applies the CFK framework to a broader class of problems - multi-dimensional options - and provides a corresponding theorem. Notably, the CFK framework can also be used to derive a second-order path-wise weak approximation for a type of average functions associated with multi-dimensional Markov processes.

The origin of cosmic diffuse gamma-ray background is a major puzzle in high-energy astronomy. Studies have shown that early investigations significantly underestimated the radiation from galaxy clusters due to the lack of accurate modeling of secondary gamma-ray production. In this research, we have revised our understanding of cosmic diffuse gamma-ray background by taking into account the precise secondary gamma-ray spectrum produced through the interaction of cosmic rays and atomic nuclei in the intercluster space. Our study indicates that early estimates of galaxy cluster contributions to the gamma-ray background were approximately double the actual value. It appears than at least 40% of the cosmic diffuse gamma-ray background can be attributed to galaxy clusters, with the remaining balance potentially accounted for by other galactic sources.

The cosmic primordial universe may harbor invisible physics beyond the Standard Model, embedded in the quantum fluctuations that occurred during its inception. This dark matter phenomenon could manifest as irregularities in the power spectrum, revealed by large-scale cosmological observations. A novel cosmological collider signal, stemming from the gravitational wave radiation emitted by heavy particles, will appear as a breaking wave pattern superimposed on the power spectrum within the source range of these heavy particles. By analyzing the resulting phenomenon on various cosmological scales, the existence of dark matter such as primordial axions or gravitationally-modulated axion dark matter within a specific mass range can be verified or discredited. This study finds that the quantum fluctuations leading to the cosmic collider signal are highly sensitive to the momentum correlations of the dark matter particles, providing valuable information regarding their physics.

Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain their decision-making processes can be highly beneficial. The problem with existing methods is that they either require specialized data, extensive processing power, or struggle to pinpoint the specific part of an image that's used to make a decision. We've proposed a new technique called LaViSE that tackles these issues by using a unique framework to pinpoint and measure the importance of specific image regions in making decisions. By using this approach, we can explain complex models using simple, visual representations, and it's based on recognizing correlations between images and text descriptions. We've tested LaViSE on various benchmarks and found that it works effectively, and it's particularly useful because it's fast, flexible, and requires minimal processing power.

Developing a simplified microscopic model of cuprate materials, we investigate how electron-phonon interactions affect the properties of one-dimensional cuprate compounds. First, it is discovered that the electron-phonon potential gives rise to a significant and deep minimum in the system's potential well, primarily attributed to third-order effects. Additionally, it is found that this interaction results in a long-range attractive coupling between Cu ions. Furthermore, using a quantum Monte Carlo method, researchers have, for the first time, directly observed a significant attraction between Cu ions in a cuprate material, thus substantiating experimental observations and providing a fundamental explanation for them. This interaction is found to be tied to the dimerization of Cu-O bonds, which in turn is driven by phonon-mediated attraction. It is also proposed that this interaction may play a crucial role in cuprate formation and the emergence of superconductivity, with the admission of phonon degrees of freedom.

The ongoing Population-based HIV Impact Assessment project aims to measure national and regional progress in combating the HIV epidemic, a primary goal of UNAIDS' 90-90-90 targets. By conducting a symposium on causal learning methods in medical research, we began exploring ways to utilize causal structural learning networks in the field of medicine. Given the symposium's focus, we chose the mobile health domain for our in-depth analysis. We introduced two methods for identifying causal relationships between variables: a discrete network learning approach grounded in the Bayesian network framework, and a continuous learning method based on the linear structural latent model. We processed the Mobile PHIs individual dataset, which comprises a total of 21 variables, along with their corresponding discrete and continuous distributions. Our findings on the MPHIA dataset indicate that both discrete and continuous networks feature a prominent sub-network centered on the 'companion' node, which is connected to significant public health issues such as violence, substance abuse, and mental health. These results mirror real-world observations, highlighting the value of causal structural learning networks in the field of medicine.

In the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$, which exhibits a unique crystal structure, researchers have identified a skyrmion type of magnetic structure. They find that skyrmions within this material undergo a first-order phase transition at elevated temperatures. This transition, which shows a significant decrease in energy at 270 K, is unusual in that it is not influenced by the presence of external fields. At temperatures just above the critical point, the researchers observe a unique "fog of skyrmions" state, which indicates a gradual approach to the critical point without a clear phase boundary. They also find that heat capacity measurements reveal a distinct peak at 270 K, which provides further evidence of the phase transition's first-order nature. Additionally, the researchers use microscopic simulations to model the phase transition and find that it shares similarities with the melting of a two-dimensional ice crystal. Finally, the researchers predict that external fields will influence the behavior of the system at lower temperatures, leading to the disappearance of the "fog of skyrmions" state.

High-dimensional dynamic factor models serve as a fundamental category of models to analyze and forecast connected time series datasets with a significant number of variables. This overview highlights essential recent breakthroughs in the field, particularly those concerning identification strategies, optimization techniques, and estimation procedures. It explores the links between these breakthroughs in high-dimensional statistics with the broader objectives of the theory and discusses potential areas of research for further investigation.

The equilibrium problem described by the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality encompasses several key problems like optimization, variational inequality, and others, as specific instances. This paper aims to provide a clear outline illustrating the connection between fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping and solutions to the equilibrium problem that satisfy particular monotonicity and Lipschitz-type constraints.

Recent breakthroughs in information hiding have led to the introduction of a new category of reversible steganography, enabling the extraction of original data alongside compressed information from a given carrier. The development of this field has been rapid due to its varied applications across fields such as machine learning, signal processing and computer vision. As with other areas of information hiding, the critical concern persists - how can the steganographic data and its extractor be trusted? Our contribution presents a reliable method for the extractor to verify the integrity of the steganographic data, its authenticity, and ensure correct working of the steganographic algorithm through a novel Bayesian neural network. The network builds upon a novel reversible steganographic framework, allowing for the extraction of not only the original data and secret information, but also the steganographic algorithm itself. The integration of the Bayesian network into the extractor has a minimal impact on the framework's transparency.

The mathematical tools used to study how turbulence affects magnetic field generation in solar and stellar interiors are being increasingly tested using three-dimensional simulations. By using self-consistent models that incorporate the effects of turbulence, it's becoming clear that previously simplified models were too limited. These earlier models, which only accounted for certain interactions, failed to capture the full range of turbulence's influence. In contrast, more comprehensive models that incorporate all turbulence effects predict a more intense magnetic field than observed in recent measurements. These more robust models also suggest that certain parameters have a greater impact on the field generation process than initially thought, and that turbulence effects vary depending on the field's geometry and scale.

A study has revealed molecular outflows in the central area of the galaxy NGC4945 using the ALMA. At a high resolution of ~0.3", the ALMA detected four distinct plumes of molecular gas, possibly corresponding to gas from different epochs. Three of these outflows, specifically those driven by ionized and ionizing gas, may have formed approximately 100 years ago and could be activated by the AGN, whereas one driven by the AGN may have occurred more recently. These outflows correspond to a specific velocity range of ~200-600 km/s and have sizes varying between 0.04 to 0.45 parsecs. Additionally, the study found an asymmetrical distribution of the galaxy's molecular material, including a specific wing, possibly resulting from outflow activity. An analysis of the wing using different tracers supports its origin from outflow phenomena. An estimate of the galaxy's gas mass revealed the presence of 1.3*10^7 solar masses, specifically corresponding to high-density gas. An analysis of the galaxy's molecular distribution reveals the presence of two distinct populations, specifically those of population I and II. A comparison of the gas mass with the solid body mass of the galaxy indicates a specific ratio, whereas the gas-to-solar ratio in NGC4945 is similar to that of the galaxy NGC4945. A simplified version of the original kinetic equation has been created to study a magnetized plasma's time-dependent behavior. This simplified model, called the quasilinear model, reduces complexity by simplifying the Boltzmann distribution into a more manageble form. Its nonlinear system of partial differential equations can be approximated using an iterative process, leading to a more linear system that can be solved using various numerical approaches. However, conventional numerical methods fail to maintain the underlying conservation laws of the original model. Researchers have developed an alternative numerical technique based on conservative finite element methods that effectively preserves key properties of the model. This numerical approach employs a high-order interpolation scheme, providing accurate predictions of the model's behavior. To ensure precision in the numerical context, a variational Monte Carlo method is utilized to maintain conservation. Its performance has been validated in model studies, demonstrating its accuracy and reliability.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

We provide a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions of a specific Lyapunov inequality in B+(X,X*), where X is a Banach space. The inequality's solutions determine the boundedness of the resolvent R(λ,A) inside and outside the left half-plane and left invertibility of T, the C0-semigroup.

This paper introduces MuMuPy, a computational program and Python module that calculates dimuonium-matter interaction probabilities, specifically for interactions with electrons, proton-pion systems and more generally for bose fields. It serves as a user-friendly alternative to the established Higgs program while maintaining compatibility with its input parameters, allowing for seamless integration into larger codes. MuMuPy, in its current form, supports a range of new features over Higgs, though the program's limitations to low-energy interactions mean it cannot match Higgs' treatment of high-energy dimuonium production. MuMuPy is distributed at no cost under the permissive MIT License, with accompanying documentation available online.

Portfolio managers assess investment success in relation to market standards, specifically using the Standard & Poor 500 index as a benchmark. Our revised assessment combines two key measures: the investor's absolute returns and their relative performance versus a chosen market index. These returns are evaluated through a utility of wealth function, which reflects how an investor gains or loses from market outcomes. Our model aligns with the principles of Kelly Capital and optimizes performance, but with a twist, as the utility function takes into consideration both absolute and relative returns. Unlike the traditional Kelly framework, which solely focuses on the investor's absolute returns due to frictional costs, our model successfully incorporates both absolute and relative returns. Our results will serve as a direct replacement for the standard Kelly model, as the principles remain largely the same, allowing investors to better position themselves in line with market standards.

The most abundant galaxy type in the cosmos is dwarf galaxies, which exhibit prominent characteristics in studies of cosmic evolution, including minimal star production, high gas abundance, and distinctive chemical development. In the realm of cosmic evolution research, dwarf galaxies play a pivotal part. Through observational studies, it has been established that the interstellar media of dwarf galaxies comprise primarily hydrogen, exist within gravitational potentials that are primarily dark matter-driven, and the kinetic energy of their gas is either negligible in comparison to its potential energy or exists in a dynamically neutral state. The presented paper aims to summarize current knowledge regarding the interstellar media within dwarf galaxies, particularly relating to the GASS and HiGas surveys, that detail the interstellar media through the measurement of neutral hydrogen. The paper also explores theoretical models of the interstellar media within dwarf galaxies, specifically the self-regulating star formation model which seeks to explain the abundance distribution of heavy elements within dwarf galaxies through the balance of star production and spheroid destruction.

We investigate the stability of fermionic quasiparticles in a system that includes both fermions and bosons that can condense. We start by considering a simplified model where the bosons do not condense, but rather interact with the fermions in a way that follows the principles of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. In this context, the quasiparticle spectrum is characterized by two distinct bands separated by a significant gap. As the fermions strongly couple to the bosons, the gap in the quasiparticle spectrum gradually diminishes, but it may eventually disappear and transform into a continuous band, blocking quasiparticle propagation. This phenomenon can be generalized to other models featuring bosons that condense and is applicable to systems with an even number of quasiparticles. We also explore the time-dependent collapse of the quasiparticle gap by initiating a process that causes the bosonic field to switch between two distinct states. Our analysis reveals that the quasiparticle gap undergoes a periodic decline and rise. Furthermore, the quasiparticle spectrum exhibits significant broadening and may merge with the continuous spectrum that emerges as a result of the bosons condensing.

Golan and Sapir \cite{MR3978542} showed that the Thompson's groups $F$, $T$, and $V$ exhibit linear divergence. The present work extends this analysis to broader classes of these groups. Specifically, we investigate the Brown-Thompson groups $F_n$, $T_n$, and $V_n$ and discover that they too have a linear divergence function. Furthermore, our research encompasses the braided Thompson groups $F^{\mathfrak{B}}$, $T^{\mathfrak{B}}$, and $V^{\mathfrak{B}}$ and establishes that they too display linear divergence.

This paper demonstrates the end-to-end fine-tuning of the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. Key technical hurdles are identified that must be overcome to accomplish this goal. A comparative evaluation is presented to show the superiority of the end-to-end RAG architecture in the context of question answering. Our implementation of the end-to-end RAG architecture has been made publicly available on the HuggingFace Transformers library.

This study calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to a specific logarithmic weight given by $\log\left(\frac{2k}{1-x}\right)$ over the interval $(-1,1)$ where $k>1$, and we verify a long-standing conjecture. The calculated long-term behavior is then applied to determine the asymptotic behavior of the degree of the best approximation in the space of polynomials that are orthogonal with respect to the specified weight.

Utilizing crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk to acquire top-tier human annotations proves more complicated than initially thought, influenced by several key factors, such as task instructions and annotator compensation, among others, which can have a significant impact on overall annotation quality. To prevent low-quality annotations from compromising the entire set, it is crucial to thoroughly evaluate each potential annotator before hiring, yet this proves impractical with limited pre-annotation available for review. To mitigate this challenge, we suggest implementing high-quality annotations as qualifying tests to ensure top-tier annotators. We examine the impact of one such qualifying test, specifically regarding text summarization, where we analyze how annotations change throughout the hiring process and how they correlate with pre-annotation quality. Our findings reveal that pre-annotation calibration is indeed effective in distinguishing high-quality from low-quality annotations, but only after the hiring candidate has completed several annotations, suggesting that pre-annotation serves as an initial filter to identify top-tier candidates, which will then produce superior results as they become more experienced.

Text-video retrieval, an essential task of practical importance, has seen escalating interest in recent times. Current methods for this task rely heavily on pre-trained models that leverage the interplay between image features and the interplay of visual and textual information. However, the majority of these models have been developed using a dual-cameras setup that merely shifts token features without addressing the task of image-text matching. Moreover, they typically employ straightforward averaging techniques to combine features without considering the task of image-text matching. 

We propose the TS2-Net, a cutting-edge approach for text-video retrieval. This method builds upon the foundation of token-based features and leverages a novel token selection mechanism, as well as a revised image-text matching framework. The TS2-Net boasts a streamlined design and relies on the efficient extraction of features from pre-trained models. The token selection mechanism empowers the model to learn task-relevant features, while the revised image-text matching framework leverages the token features effectively to achieve superior performance. 

The TS2-Net has been validated using the MSRVTT, VCOCT, ActivityNet, and DiDeMo benchmark datasets. The results indicate significant performance enhancements over current state-of-the-art methods with minimal additional processing requirements. For instance, on the MSRVTT dataset, the TS2-Net has achieved a remarkable 82.7% ranked-based recall, surpassing the previous best-performing method by a substantial margin of 2.1%.
